If the group reaches an agreement, staff write it down in plain words or pictures, check that each person agrees, and note the date. The individuals can change or end the agreement at any time.
If no agreement is reached, staff try other options, may ask the Program Specialist to help, and offer a trusted advocate to any individual who wants one.
The Program Specialist reviews unresolved differences within [3] working days, meets with the individuals, and may involve the individuals' team members and families as the individuals wish.

When a choice might create significant health or safety risk, the Program Specialist and the team assess the risk, discuss it with the individual, and look for ways to lower the risk (for example, supports, supervision, adaptations) while keeping the choice. A limit is considered only through the process in IR-02.
Where the conflict involves shared bedrooms, the Program Specialist uses the same process, and a roommate change is made only with the consent of the individuals affected (see PS-01 and PG-01).
Staff do not use negotiation to move any individual out of the home. If a conflict leads to a possible transfer, the process in PG-04 applies.

If a conflict involves threats, harm or abuse, staff stop the behavior, protect everyone, notify the Administrator immediately, and handle it as an incident under GR-04 and GR-05, not as a negotiation.

Staff record each significant negotiation, including the choices, options considered, outcome and each person's agreement, in the daily documentation (PG-02) for each affected individual, and the Program Specialist includes any recurring issue in the person-centered plan.
Individuals may use the grievance procedure (GR-09) if unhappy with an outcome. No one is retaliated against for raising a choice or disagreement.

The Program Specialist reviews negotiation records quarterly to spot patterns, such as repeated conflicts about the same issue, and reports them to the Administrator for the quality improvement review (GOV-02).
Staff are trained on this procedure in orientation and annually (ST-03, ST-04).

responsibilities.duty: Supports negotiations that staff cannot resolve, assesses health and safety questions, and reviews records quarterly.
Notice conflicts, support each individual's voice, stay neutral, record outcomes and report concerns.
Ensures no rights are violated in outcomes and that patterns are addressed.
Express their choices and take part in finding options, with an advocate if wanted.

documentation: Negotiation notes in daily documentation for each affected individual
Written agreements (plain-language or pictures) with date and signatures where possible
Program Specialist review notes
Person-centered plan updates for recurring issues
Quarterly pattern review
Incident reports when conflicts involve harm

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors and board members of [AGENCY NAME] who create, use, see or disclose information about an individual receiving services in the community home.
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of each individual's records and personal information, to limit who may see or receive that information, and to meet the Pennsylvania record access and release requirements and the HIPAA Privacy and Breach Notification Rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats every individual's records and personal information as confidential. Privacy is one of the individual's rights under 55 Pa. Code §6400.32, and this policy is applied together with the rights policies (IR-01 and IR-02). Individual records are accessible only to the persons authorized under §6400.216. Information is released outside the agency only with the consent required under §6400.217, or where a law or regulation requires or permits disclosure and the Privacy Officer has approved it. As a HIPAA covered entity, [AGENCY NAME] follows 45 CFR 164.530 (administrative requirements), 164.502 (uses and disclosures, including the minimum necessary standard), 164.524 (individual access to records) and 164.400-414 (breach notification). [AGENCY NAME] appoints a Privacy Officer, gives each individual a notice of privacy practices and trains all staff. Staff share only the information they need to do their jobs, and never discuss an individual's information in public places, on social media or in unsecured text messages or email.

definitions.definition: A person who receives residential services from [AGENCY NAME] in the community home.
Individually identifiable health or other personal information about an individual, in any form (paper, electronic or spoken), that is held by the agency.

A person permitted to see an individual's record under §6400.216, such as the individual, the individual's legal representative or someone with a valid consent, staff who need the record to perform their duties, and regulatory or oversight personnel with legal authority.
An acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI not permitted by the HIPAA Privacy Rule that compromises the security or privacy of the information, as defined in 45 CFR 164.402.
The least amount of information needed to accomplish the purpose of a use or disclosure (45 CFR 164.502(b)).

procedures: The Governing Body or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] appoints a Privacy Officer in writing and records the name and contact information ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]) in the policy manual and in the notice of privacy practices.

The Privacy Officer maintains a list of authorized persons by role (for example direct support staff, nurse, program specialist, CEO, fiscal staff) showing which parts of the record each role may see, consistent with §6400.216. The list is reviewed at least annually.

Before or at admission, the Program Specialist gives each individual (and legal representative, if any) the agency's notice of privacy practices in a format and language the person understands (see IR-05), explains it, and files a signed acknowledgment in the record. If the person or representative refuses to sign, staff document the attempt and the date.

All staff sign a confidentiality statement at hire and complete HIPAA privacy training during orientation (ST-03) and again at least annually (ST-04). The Privacy Officer keeps training dates and sign-in sheets.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets or a locked office, and the home's current-record folder is kept where authorized staff can reach it but visitors cannot. Electronic records require individual log-ins, passwords and screen locks. Staff do not share passwords.
Staff access, use or disclose only the minimum necessary PHI for their task. Anyone who views a record without a job-related need is reported to the Privacy Officer.

Before releasing any information to someone outside the agency, staff confirm either (a) a valid signed consent from the individual or legal representative that meets the content requirements of §6400.217, or (b) that the disclosure is required or permitted by law and has been approved by the Privacy Officer. The Privacy Officer confirms the consent form's content against the rule text and updates the form if needed. Consents are dated, name the recipient and the information to be released, and have an expiration date.

Staff record every release outside routine treatment, payment and operations in the individual's record, noting the date, recipient, information released, purpose and the staff member who released it (see REC-02).

When an individual or legal representative asks to see or get a copy of the record, staff give the request to the Privacy Officer the same day. Under 45 CFR 164.524 the Privacy Officer acts on the request no later than 30 days after receipt (one 30-day extension is allowed with a written explanation). The request and the response are documented.
If access is denied in whole or part, the Privacy Officer gives a written denial that states the basis and explains the review and complaint rights that apply.

Staff do not discuss an individual's information in common areas where others can overhear. Names, diagnoses and medication information are not posted where visitors can see them, except as needed for safety (for example allergy information stored out of public view).

Photographs, video or audio recordings of an individual and any use of an individual's name or image in publicity or social media require specific written consent from the individual or legal representative. Staff do not post about individuals on personal social media.

Staff who suspect a privacy or security incident (misdirected fax or email, lost record, lost phone or laptop, unauthorized access) report it to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the shift.
The Privacy Officer investigates within 5 business days, performs and documents a risk assessment under 45 CFR 164.402, and decides whether a reportable breach occurred.

For a reportable breach, [AGENCY NAME] notifies each affected individual (or representative) in writing without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. It also notifies the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the media where 45 CFR 164.400-414 requires it. The Privacy Officer keeps the breach log and all notices.

Where the privacy event is also an incident under the agency's incident reporting policy, the Privacy Officer and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] coordinate so that incident reporting requirements are met (see GR-04).

Individuals and representatives may file a privacy complaint with the agency (see GR-09) or with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. No one may be retaliated against for filing a complaint.
Staff who violate this policy are subject to corrective action up to and including termination under the agency's sanctions policy. The Privacy Officer documents the sanctions applied.

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy at least annually and keeps HIPAA documentation, including policies, acknowledgments, training and breach records, for at least 6 years under 45 CFR 164.530(j), or longer if another retention rule applies (see REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Appoint the Privacy Officer, approve this policy, provide resources for safeguards and enforce sanctions.
Maintain the authorized-person list, handle access requests, approve non-routine disclosures, investigate privacy incidents and breaches, run training and keep HIPAA documentation.
Give and explain the notice of privacy practices at admission and file the signed acknowledgment.

responsibilities.role: Direct support staff and all other staff
responsibilities.duty: Protect PHI, access only what is needed, obtain consent before release, and report suspected privacy incidents immediately.

documentation: Notice of privacy practices and signed acknowledgments
Signed consents for release of information (§6400.217)
Log of disclosures and record access requests, with responses
Authorized-person list under §6400.216
Staff confidentiality statements and HIPAA training records
Privacy incident reports, risk assessments and breach log with notices
Sanctions documentation and annual policy review record

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME] and all applicants, individuals, legal representatives and family members who seek or receive services in the community home.
policies.purpose: To make sure that no one is denied admission or services, or treated differently, because of disability type, race, national origin or religion, and that individuals and their representatives can understand and be understood in every part of their services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission or in the delivery of services on the basis of the type of disability, race, national origin or religion. This policy supports the individual rights listed in 55 Pa. Code §6400.32 and complies with Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (28 CFR Part 36) and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (45 CFR Part 80). [AGENCY NAME] provides interpreters, auxiliary aids and services, and translated materials at no cost to the individual or representative. Each individual's preferred method of communication is identified and written into the individual's plan, and staff are trained to use it. Admission decisions are based on the agency's documented ability to meet the person's needs and the home's licensed capacity, not on a protected characteristic (see PG-01).

definitions.definition: Supports that allow effective communication, such as qualified sign language interpreters, large print, braille, picture or symbol systems, communication devices, captioning, and plain-language or easy-read materials.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English that requires language assistance to take part meaningfully in services.
The way an individual expresses and understands information, such as speech, gestures, signs, pictures, devices, behavior or a combination.

A person who is able to interpret accurately, effectively and impartially, using specialized vocabulary if needed. A family member or another individual living in the home is not used as an interpreter except at the person's own informed request when no qualified interpreter is needed for safety or accuracy.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates a Nondiscrimination and Access Coordinator, named in the policy manual with contact information ([PHONE]), to receive questions and complaints about this policy.

At referral and admission, staff ask each applicant and representative about the person's communication method, language and any aids needed, and they record the answers on the admission checklist (see PG-01).

Admission and service decisions are reviewed by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] against written criteria that relate only to the agency's ability to meet the person's needs and available capacity. A decision not to admit is documented with the reasons, and the documentation is checked to confirm that disability type, race, national origin or religion played no part.

The Program Specialist records the individual's communication method in the individual plan, including how the person expresses choices, yes/no, pain, distress and refusal, and what aids or devices the person uses. The plan is updated when the person's communication changes (see PG-02).

Staff are trained on each individual's communication method during orientation and plan review. New staff are not left to work alone with an individual until they have been shown how that person communicates.

When an individual or representative needs an interpreter, staff arrange a qualified interpreter (sign language, spoken language or other) at no charge. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a list of interpreter and translation vendors, including a telephone or video interpreter service, at [PHONE], in the home's office.

Important documents, including the notice of privacy practices, rights information, grievance procedure, consents and plan summaries, are provided in the individual's language and in an accessible format (plain language, large print, pictures or audio) on request and without charge. The Program Specialist records the date each was provided.

Staff explain rights, consents and plan content in a way the individual can understand and check the person's understanding. If the person cannot understand, staff involve the legal representative while still including the individual to the fullest extent possible (see IR-02).

Assistive technology and communication devices are kept charged, in working order and available at all times. Staff report broken devices to the Program Specialist the same day, who arranges repair or replacement.

Staff may not refuse service, treat a person differently, restrict visitors or activities, or make negative remarks because of the person's disability type, race, national origin, religion or language. Observed or suspected discrimination is reported to the Nondiscrimination Coordinator the same day.

The Coordinator documents every report or complaint, reviews it within 5 business days, takes corrective action and informs the complainant of the outcome. Complaints are also processed under the grievance policy (see GR-09). No retaliation is permitted against anyone who raises a concern.

Individuals may request reasonable modifications to home practices (for example schedule or format changes) because of a disability. The Program Specialist considers each request, documents the decision and the reason, and informs the person in an accessible format.
The home's physical access needs are addressed under the environment policy (see PS-01), and visitors with disabilities are given the access and communication supports they need.
Nondiscrimination and communication access are included in staff orientation and annual training (ST-03, ST-04).
[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews this policy and a sample of communication-access records at least annually, and the results are reported to the Governing Body (see GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure nondiscriminatory admission decisions, fund interpreters and aids, and review this policy annually.
Receive, document and resolve complaints and requests for accommodations.
Identify and document each person's communication method in the plan and arrange translated or accessible materials and interpreters.
Use each person's documented communication method, keep devices working and report discrimination or access barriers.

documentation: Admission checklist with communication and language needs
Individual plan section describing the person's communication method
Records of interpreter and auxiliary-aid requests and services provided
Dated record of translated or accessible materials provided
Reasons for any non-admission decision
Discrimination complaints and resolutions
Annual policy review

policies.title: Chief Executive Officer and Program Specialist Qualifications
policies.applies_to: The Governing Body, the Chief Executive Officer, the Program Specialist(s) and anyone who hires or supervises them at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has a qualified Chief Executive Officer and enough qualified Program Specialists at all times, and that qualifications are verified and kept on file.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs one Chief Executive Officer (CEO) who meets 55 Pa. Code §6400.43: a master's degree plus 2 years, or a bachelor's degree plus 4 years, of administration or human-services experience. The agency also employs one Program Specialist for every 30 individuals served, as required by §6400.44. Each Program Specialist has a bachelor's degree plus 2 years of experience working directly with individuals with an intellectual disability or autism, or a master's degree plus 1 year of that experience, or an associate degree or 60 college credits plus 4 years of that experience, as described in the ODP 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide. Separately from licensing, ODP waiver provider enrollment requires an executive with a bachelor's degree and 5 years of residential management experience. [AGENCY NAME] confirms that its executive meets this enrollment standard in addition to §6400.43. A person is not placed in either position until qualifications are verified and documented.

definitions.definition: The person responsible for the overall administration and operation of the agency and of the home, named in the organizational chart. For purposes of §6400.43 the CEO must meet the education and experience standard above.

The qualified staff person responsible for the program aspects of services, including assessment, development and oversight of the individual plan. The agency employs at least one Program Specialist for every 30 individuals.

Paid or documented volunteer experience providing services to or working directly with individuals with an intellectual disability or autism, as defined for Program Specialists in §6400.44 and the ODP guide.
Experience in administration, management or delivery of human services that is relevant to the CEO's duties.

procedures: The Governing Body approves a written job description for the CEO and for the Program Specialist. Each describes duties, reporting line, and the minimum education and experience required under §6400.43 and §6400.44.
[AGENCY NAME] maintains an organizational chart that names the CEO, Program Specialist(s) and all supervisory positions, shows reporting relationships, and is updated within 30 days of any change.
Before an offer is made, the hiring authority (the Governing Body for the CEO; the CEO for the Program Specialist) checks the candidate's résumé and application against the minimum qualifications.
For each candidate, the agency obtains an official or verified copy of the degree or transcript, confirming the degree level and, for the associate/60-credit option, the number of credits.

The agency contacts prior employers or other sources to verify the dates, duties and number of years of experience. For the Program Specialist, the verification must show direct experience with individuals with an intellectual disability or autism. Verification is documented on a dated qualification worksheet.

For the CEO, the hiring authority also confirms that the person meets the ODP waiver enrollment standard of a bachelor's degree and 5 years of residential management experience, and records the result. Where the CEO does not meet that standard, the agency designates another executive who does and records that person in the personnel file and the enrollment application (see GOV-01).

The hiring authority completes the qualification worksheet, signs and dates it, and files it in the personnel file along with the degree or transcript, the experience verification, the job description and the criminal history documentation required by GR-07.
Neither position is filled by a person whose qualifications cannot be verified. The agency does not rely on a verbal statement alone.

The Governing Body calculates annually and at each admission whether the number of Program Specialists is sufficient for the number of individuals served (1 per 30). When the census approaches a multiple of 30, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] starts recruitment early so that the ratio is never exceeded.

If the CEO or the Program Specialist leaves, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] notifies the Governing Body within 1 business day and names a qualified interim person within 7 days. The interim person's qualifications are verified and documented the same way. Applicable notification requirements to ODP are reviewed with GOV-01.
A person who is promoted into either position is verified against the same standards before the change takes effect.
The Governing Body reviews the CEO's and the Program Specialist's qualification files, job descriptions and the organizational chart at least annually and records the review in its minutes.

Both the CEO and the Program Specialist complete the annual training required for their positions under ST-04. Management and administrative staff complete 12 hours, and Program Specialists complete 24 hours.

responsibilities.duty: Approve job descriptions, hire and verify the CEO, confirm the ODP enrollment executive standard and review qualifications annually.
Hire and verify Program Specialists, keep the organizational chart current and maintain the program specialist-to-individual ratio.
Maintain proof of qualifications in the personnel file and complete required training.
Collect and file degree, transcript and experience verification before the start date.

documentation: Job descriptions for CEO and Program Specialist
Organizational chart with revision dates
Qualification worksheet with degree/transcript and experience verification
Documentation of ODP enrollment executive qualification
Annual Governing Body review of qualifications and program specialist ratio
Interim appointment records, if any

policies.title: Staffing Ratios, Supervision and Awake Overnight Staff
policies.applies_to: The CEO, Program Specialist, home supervisors, scheduling staff and all direct support staff of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure enough qualified staff of legal age are present and awake in the home at all times to meet minimum ratios and each individual's plan, and that supervision and backup coverage are in place for every shift.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] staffs each home with at least 1 staff person for every 8 individuals while individuals are awake and present, and at least 1 staff person for every 16 individuals while individuals are sleeping, as required by 55 Pa. Code §6400.45(b). When an individual's plan calls for staffing or staff qualifications above the minimum, [AGENCY NAME] implements the plan as written (§6400.45(d)). Staff counted in the ratio must be 18 years of age or older (§6400.42). [AGENCY NAME] does not assume that a staff person may sleep during the overnight shift. For each home, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms and documents whether the awake-staff requirement in §6400.232 applies, and until that confirmation is made the agency schedules awake overnight staff. A staff person counted in the ratio must be awake. [AGENCY NAME] keeps an on-call and backup coverage roster so no shift falls below the ratio.

definitions.definition: Staff physically in the home, awake and able to respond, while individuals are awake and present.
The hours when individuals are asleep. The ratio of 1 staff to 16 individuals applies while individuals sleep and are physically present.
A staff person who is awake and alert throughout the overnight shift and is counted in the ratio.
A staff person who is at least 18 years old and is counted toward the minimum ratio.
A written list of on-call staff, with phone numbers, who can cover absences.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Program Specialist set the minimum staffing for each home by dividing the number of individuals present by 8 (awake) and by 16 (sleeping), rounding up to a whole staff person. They then compare the result with the staffing in each individual plan and use whichever is higher.

The Program Specialist writes each individual's required staffing level and any special staff qualifications (for example behavior support or medical training) into the individual plan. The scheduler transfers these requirements to the home's master schedule, and the plan requirement is implemented as written.

The scheduler prepares a written schedule at least 2 weeks ahead for each home that shows, for every hour of the day, the names of the staff, the number of individuals expected to be present, and the required ratio. The schedule is posted at the home's office and kept on file.

Before a person is placed on a schedule as counted staff, the scheduler confirms from the personnel file that the person is at least 18 years old (§6400.42) and has completed the orientation required before working alone (ST-03) and the criminal history requirements (GR-07). No one under 18 is counted in the ratio.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms in writing, for each home, whether the §6400.232 awake-staff requirement applies, and records the basis for the conclusion. Until confirmed, the home is scheduled with at least one awake staff person overnight. A staff person counted in the ratio is awake for the whole shift and does not sleep on duty.

Overnight staff complete and sign an overnight log at the start and end of the shift. The log shows the time of each check on individuals, any events and the staff person's name. The supervisor reviews the logs weekly.

The scheduler maintains a backup coverage roster with at least [NUMBER] qualified, background-checked on-call staff per home, including the supervisor and the Program Specialist, with current phone numbers. The roster is posted in the home and reviewed monthly.

A staff person who cannot report for a shift calls the supervisor or on-call number at [PHONE] as soon as the problem is known and no later than 2 hours before the shift, unless there is an emergency. The on-call person calls staff from the backup roster until the shift is covered.

The staff person on duty must not leave the home until a relief staff person arrives and receives a verbal and written handoff. If relief does not arrive, the staff person stays and notifies the supervisor immediately. The supervisor arranges coverage within 1 hour.

If a shift cannot be filled and the ratio cannot be met, the supervisor notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] immediately. The CEO or Program Specialist, if qualified and background-checked, works the shift or other arrangements are made. The event is documented and reviewed as a staffing failure (see GOV-02).

When individuals are out of the home, the supervisor confirms that those who stay at the home are still covered at the required ratio and that those in the community have the staffing their plans require. Daily assignments are written on the shift sheet.

Supervisors observe each direct support staff person on shift in each home at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., monthly], check that the schedule is followed, and document the observation. Findings are discussed with the staff person.

Payroll or time records are used to confirm that actual staffing matched the schedule. The supervisor reviews the daily time records against the schedule weekly and reports any shortfalls to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
Staff in the home are given the emergency, on-call and supervisor numbers, and know who to call for help with a medical, behavioral or safety emergency (see FS-02 and IH-02).
When a new person moves into the home or an individual's needs change, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] recalculates staffing before the move or change and adds staff first if required.

Every quarter, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews schedules, overnight logs, call-outs and time records, and reports to the Governing Body on whether staffing met the ratios and the plan requirements (see GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Set and fund staffing, confirm the awake-staff determination for each home and review staffing quarterly.
Write plan staffing requirements and make sure the schedule implements them.
Build schedules that meet the ratios, check staff age and clearance, and maintain the backup roster.
Cover absences, review logs, observe staff and report shortfalls.
Stay awake and present during assigned shifts, hand off properly and give prompt notice of an absence.

documentation: Written schedules showing staff and ratios for each shift
Individual plan staffing requirements
Evidence of staff age in the personnel file
Written determination about the §6400.232 awake-staff requirement for each home
Overnight logs and shift handoff notes
Backup and on-call roster
Time records, shortfall reports and quarterly staffing review

policies.title: Staff Orientation Program
policies.applies_to: All newly hired staff of [AGENCY NAME], and the supervisors and trainers who conduct or verify orientation.
policies.purpose: To make sure every new staff person completes the orientation required by the regulation before working alone with individuals and within 30 days of hire, and that the content and attendance are documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a written orientation program to each newly hired staff person. The orientation must be completed before the person works alone with individuals and within 30 days after hire, as described in 55 Pa. Code §6400.51 and the ODP 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide. This policy meets 55 Pa. Code §6400.51(b), Part B (orientation plan), item 51b1-5 (RCG p.59). The orientation encompasses: (1) the application of person-centered practices, community integration, individual choice, and supporting individuals to develop and maintain relationships; (2) the prevention, detection and reporting of abuse, suspected abuse and alleged abuse in accordance with the Older Adults Protective Services Act (35 P.S. §§ 10225.101-10225.5102), the Child Protective Services Law (23 Pa.C.S. §§ 6301-6386), the Adult Protective Services Act (35 P.S. §§ 10210.101-10210.704) and applicable protective services regulations; (3) individual rights; (4) recognizing and reporting incidents; and (5) job-related knowledge and skills. [AGENCY NAME] applies this orientation to all new staff, whatever their role, and does not count a person as working alone, or in the staffing ratio, until orientation is complete.

definitions.definition: The structured introduction that every new staff person must complete before working alone with individuals and within 30 days of hire.
Providing care or supervision to an individual without another fully oriented staff person present.
The written curriculum, with objectives, content, method, hours and trainer, covering the five required areas.
Training specific to the person's job, such as the individual plans, medication and health procedures, emergency procedures, behavior supports and documentation.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Program Specialist maintain a written orientation plan that has a module for each of the five required areas: (1) person-centered practices, community integration, individual choice and supporting relationships; (2) abuse prevention, detection and reporting; (3) individual rights; (4) recognizing and reporting incidents; and (5) job-related knowledge and skills. The plan states the content, hours, method and trainer for each module.

On the first day of employment, the supervisor gives the new staff person the orientation schedule showing the date by which each module will be completed. The schedule must show completion within 30 days of the hire date.

Before the person works alone with any individual, the Program Specialist or supervisor confirms that the orientation required to work alone has been completed. The staff person is scheduled only alongside an oriented staff person until the sign-off is recorded, and is not counted in the staffing ratio (ST-02) until then.

Module 1 (person-centered practices) covers how [AGENCY NAME] supports individual choice, community integration and relationships, including review of each person's plan and preferences, and links to PG-02, PG-03 and IR-03.

Module 2 (abuse) covers the signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation; who must report; the staff person's duty as a mandated reporter; reporting procedures under the Older Adults Protective Services Act, the Child Protective Services Law and the Adult Protective Services Act, and applicable protective services regulations; the agency's abuse prohibition policy; and protection from retaliation (see GR-03).
Module 3 (rights) covers the rights of individuals listed in §6400.32, how rights are informed and protected, and how rights restrictions are handled (see IR-01 and IR-02).
Module 4 (incidents) covers how to recognize an incident, the first response, who to notify, how to complete the incident report, and the time limits (see GR-04 and GR-05).

Module 5 (job-related knowledge and skills) covers the position's duties, the individual plans of the people the person will support, communication methods, emergency and evacuation procedures, health and medication rules appropriate to the job, behavior supports, record-keeping and confidentiality (see IR-04, FS-02, IH-02, MD-01 and RP-03).

Trainers use sign-in sheets and a written or practical check of understanding for each module. If the staff person does not demonstrate understanding, the trainer repeats the module and documents the retraining.
The trainer and the staff person sign and date the sign-in sheet for each module, and the supervisor records the completion date on an orientation checklist.

When all modules are completed, the supervisor signs the orientation completion form and sends the form, sign-in sheets and the curriculum used to the personnel file within 5 business days (see ST-06).

Each week, the Program Specialist reviews a list of all staff hired in the last 30 days and the status of their orientation. If a staff person is on day 20 and not finished, the Program Specialist arranges the remaining modules.

If orientation is not completed within 30 days, the supervisor removes the person from direct work and notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] the same day. The person does not return to unsupervised duties until orientation is complete. The reason is documented and reviewed under GOV-02.
The Program Specialist reviews the orientation plan at least annually and after any change to the regulations or to the agency's policies, and updates the curriculum accordingly.

responsibilities.duty: Approve the orientation plan and ensure that no one works alone before completing orientation.
Maintain the curriculum, conduct or arrange training and monitor 30-day completion.
Schedule new staff with oriented staff, record completion and sign off before solo work.
Attend and complete all modules and sign the sign-in sheets.

documentation: Written orientation plan and curriculum covering items 51b1-5
Orientation schedule and checklist
Sign-in sheets with dates, hours, trainer names and signatures
Records of understanding checks and retraining
Orientation completion form in the personnel file
Weekly new-hire orientation status list

policies.title: Annual Staff Training Plan
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME] (direct service workers, supervisors, program specialists, management, administrative and fiscal staff), and the Program Specialist and CEO who plan and oversee training.
policies.purpose: To make sure each staff person receives the required annual training hours on the required topics, and that the training year and records are defined and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires 24 hours of training each year for direct service workers, supervisors and program specialists, and 12 hours each year for management, administrative and fiscal staff, as described in 55 Pa. Code §6400.52 and the ODP 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide. [AGENCY NAME] establishes the dates of its training year in writing. This policy meets 55 Pa. Code §6400.52, Part B (annual training plan), item 52c1-6 (RCG p.61; the RCG labels this paragraph '6400.52(b)'). The annual training hours encompass: (1) the application of person-centered practices, community integration, individual choice and supporting individuals to develop and maintain relationships; (2) the prevention, detection and reporting of abuse, suspected abuse and alleged abuse in accordance with the Older Adults Protective Services Act (35 P.S. §§ 10225.101-10225.5102), the Child Protective Services Law (23 Pa.C.S. §§ 6301-6386), the Adult Protective Services Act (35 P.S. §§ 10210.101-10210.704) and applicable adult protective services regulations; (3) individual rights; (4) recognizing and reporting incidents; (5) the safe and appropriate use of behavior supports, if the person works directly with an individual; and (6) implementation of the individual plan, if the person works directly with an individual. Training is recorded as required by §6400.50. Fire safety, first aid, Heimlich and CPR training, and other training required under separate policies, are provided as described in ST-05 and the policies referenced there.

definitions.definition: The 12-month period, set in writing by [AGENCY NAME], within which each staff person must complete the required annual hours. [AGENCY NAME]'s training year runs from [TRAINING YEAR START DATE] to [TRAINING YEAR END DATE].
A staff person who works directly with individuals and provides care, support or supervision.
The written plan that lists the required topics, the hours, the delivery method, the trainers and the schedule for the training year.
Strategies used to support an individual's positive behavior as described in the individual plan (see RP-03).

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] sets the dates of the training year in writing, records them in this policy and tells all staff. The dates are changed only by written notice with an explanation of how the transition year will be handled.

By [DATE, e.g., 30 days before the training year begins], the Program Specialist prepares the annual training plan. The plan lists, for each job category, the required hours (24 for direct service workers, supervisors and program specialists; 12 for management, administrative and fiscal staff) and the topics, dates, trainers and methods.

The plan includes the six required content areas: (1) person-centered practices, community integration, individual choice and relationships; (2) abuse prevention, detection and reporting under the Older Adults Protective Services Act, the Child Protective Services Law, the Adult Protective Services Act and applicable regulations; (3) individual rights; (4) recognizing and reporting incidents; (5) the safe and appropriate use of behavior supports; and (6) implementation of the individual plan. Items 5 and 6 are required for anyone who works directly with an individual, and the agency also includes them in the plan for any supervisor or program specialist who works directly with individuals.

The Program Specialist updates the content each year to reflect changes in the individuals served, results of incident analysis (GR-06), quality improvement findings (GOV-02), changes in regulations, and any staff performance concerns.

The training plan includes the individual-specific training that direct staff need on each person's individual plan, including communication methods, health needs, supports and any rights restrictions or behavior support components, and it is repeated when a plan changes (see PG-02, IR-02 and RP-03).

At the start of the training year, the Program Specialist gives each staff person a training record showing the hours required for the job category and the hours completed, and gives supervisors a roster of the staff on their teams.

Training may be delivered in person, by qualified outside trainers or online, if the course has stated content and hours and the staff person's completion is documented. Qualified trainers are chosen by the Program Specialist and their credentials or experience are filed.

Staff sign in for every training session. The record shows the date, topic, number of hours, trainer name and the staff person's signature. Records for outside training include the certificate or attendance record.

Orientation hours under ST-03 are not counted toward the annual hours unless [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms in writing, with ODP, that they may be counted. For staff hired during the training year, the Program Specialist schedules the annual hours so that the full required hours are completed by the end of the training year, unless ODP guidance confirmed in writing allows otherwise.
Staff who work in more than one category are assigned the higher number of hours required.

Each month, the Program Specialist reviews the training records and gives supervisors a list of staff who are behind. Staff who have completed less than half the required hours by the middle of the training year receive a written reminder and a schedule for makeup.
Supervisors give staff paid time to attend required training. Training time is scheduled so that staffing ratios are maintained (ST-02).

A staff person who does not complete the required hours by the end of the training year is not scheduled for solo shifts [OR: is placed on a corrective action plan] until the deficit is made up. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] approves each exception in writing, and the shortfall is documented and reported to the Governing Body (see GOV-02).
The Program Specialist enters all training records in the personnel or training file within 5 business days of the training, as required by §6400.50 (see ST-06).

At the end of the training year, the Program Specialist prepares a summary report showing, for each staff person, the hours completed and the topics covered. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews the report, and the plan for the next year is based on gaps identified.

responsibilities.duty: Set the training year in writing, fund and approve the plan, approve exceptions and review the annual summary.
Write and update the training plan, arrange trainers, track hours monthly and keep training records.
Schedule paid training time, follow up on missed hours and ensure staff apply training in practice.
Complete the required hours and topics in the training year and sign in for all training.

documentation: Written training-year dates
Annual training plan covering items 52c1-6 by job category
Individual staff training records showing hours required and completed
Sign-in sheets, certificates and trainer credentials
Monthly training status reports and makeup schedules
Written exceptions and corrective actions
Annual training summary report

policies.title: Fire Safety, First Aid, Heimlich and CPR Training
policies.applies_to: All program specialists, direct service workers, relief and substitute staff, and the Administrator who supervise or work directly with individuals at any [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To make sure every program specialist and direct service worker knows how to prevent and respond to a fire and can give first aid, abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) and CPR before they work alone with individuals, and that this training is kept current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] trains every program specialist and direct service worker in fire safety before that person works with individuals. The training is repeated every year. Staff also complete first aid, Heimlich and CPR training within 6 months after hire and every year after that. Certificates are kept in the personnel file. This policy meets 55 Pa. Code §6400.46(a), Regulatory Compliance Guide p.56, official checklist item 46a. Item 46a requires that, before working with individuals, staff are trained in each of the following. (1) General fire safety. (2) Evacuation procedures. (3) Responsibilities during fire drills. (4) The designated meeting place outside the building, or within the fire safe area, in the event of an actual fire. (5) Smoking safety procedures if individuals or staff persons smoke at the home. (6) The use of fire extinguishers, smoke detectors and fire alarms. (7) Notification of the local fire department as soon as possible after a fire is discovered. Each of these seven topics is a required part of the training described below. Annual repetition of fire safety training and the first aid, Heimlich and CPR requirements are covered in the procedures. They are in addition to item 46a and follow §6400.46 and the ODP guide.

definitions.definition: Any employee, including relief and agency staff, who provides direct care, support or supervision to individuals.
The outside location, or fire safe area inside the building, that is named in the home's evacuation plan where everyone gathers after evacuating.
An area of the building identified in the evacuation plan as safe for individuals to gather during an actual fire.
Abdominal thrusts and other choking-relief techniques taught in a first aid or CPR course.

procedures: The Administrator or designee schedules fire safety training for each new program specialist and direct service worker during orientation and before the person works with individuals (see ST-03).
The trainer reviews general fire safety: fire prevention, hazards in the home, and what to do on discovering a fire (alert others, get individuals out, call 911).

The trainer walks the new employee through the home's evacuation procedures, including primary and secondary exits and the support each individual needs to evacuate, from the posted plan and each person's emergency information (see FS-02, REC-01).
The trainer reviews the employee's responsibilities during fire drills, including how drills are run, who assists whom, and documentation of the drill (see FS-03).

The trainer shows the employee the designated meeting place outside the building, or the fire safe area, for each home where the employee works, and explains how to account for every individual there.

If any individual or staff person smokes at the home, the trainer covers smoking safety procedures. If no one smokes at the home, the Administrator records this on the training record so the topic is documented as not applicable (see FS-04).

The trainer demonstrates the home's fire extinguishers, smoke detectors and fire alarms: where they are, how to use an extinguisher, what an alarm or detector sounds like, and what to do when a detector sounds or is inoperative (see FS-01).
The trainer explains that the fire department is notified as soon as possible after a fire is discovered, who makes the call, and what information to give.

The employee completes a hands-on walk-through of the home. The trainer confirms the employee can state the seven topics above. The employee and trainer sign and date the training record before the employee works with individuals.

Fire safety training is repeated for each program specialist and direct service worker every year. The Administrator sets the due date from the original training date and records it on the training tracker.
Within 6 months after hire, each employee completes first aid, Heimlich and CPR training from a recognized provider that includes hands-on skills practice. The training is repeated every year.
Until a new employee has completed first aid, Heimlich and CPR, the Administrator schedules shifts so that a staff person with current certification is present whenever that employee is working.
The employee gives a copy of each certificate or completion record to the Administrator within 5 days of completing the course. The Administrator files it in the personnel file (see ST-06).
The Administrator or designee reviews the training tracker monthly. Items due in the next 60 days are scheduled, and overdue items are reported to the CEO.

An employee whose first aid, Heimlich or CPR certification has lapsed is not counted as the only trained staff person on a shift. The Administrator schedules the employee for retraining at the earliest class available.
Relief, substitute and agency staff must complete the same fire safety orientation for each home before working there. Their certificates are copied to the home's files.

responsibilities.duty: Schedule training, make sure no employee works with individuals before fire safety training, review the tracker monthly and keep certificates on file.
Deliver the seven required fire safety topics, demonstrate equipment and the meeting place, and sign the training record.

responsibilities.role: Program specialists and direct service workers
responsibilities.duty: Attend training, complete it on time, give copies of certificates to the Administrator and apply the training in drills and emergencies.
Make sure training time and funds are provided and review overdue training reports.

documentation: Fire safety training record for each employee: topics covered, date, trainer and employee signatures
First aid, Heimlich and CPR certificates in the personnel file
Training tracker with next due dates
Record that smoking safety was covered or was not applicable to the home

policies.title: Personnel and Training Records
policies.applies_to: Administrator, CEO, human resources designee, and all employees of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep a complete, accurate and accessible personnel file and training record for every employee, so the agency can show a surveyor that each person is qualified, cleared and trained.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file and a training record for every employee, including the CEO, program specialists, direct support staff, and relief staff. Training records are maintained as required by 55 Pa. Code §6400.50. Records include hire date, orientation, annual training hours, first aid and CPR dates, TB documentation and background check dates. At adoption of this policy, the Administrator confirms the content and retention requirements in the text of §6400.50 and records the confirmed retention period in REC-02. Until confirmed, records are kept for at least the period of employment. The agency also keeps job descriptions and evidence of qualifications for the CEO, program specialist and direct support staff.

definitions.definition: The confidential file for each employee, holding hiring, qualification, clearance, health and training documents.
The record of each training event: topic, date, hours, trainer and employee signature.
A spreadsheet or system that lists every employee's training and clearance due dates.

procedures: The Administrator opens a personnel file for each employee on the date of hire and completes the file checklist before the employee's first shift alone with individuals.

The file holds the application, résumé, written job description and signed acknowledgment of duties, and evidence of qualifications. For the CEO this is education and experience records. For the program specialist it is education and experience records showing the required degree and direct experience working with individuals with an intellectual disability or autism. For direct support staff it is proof of age (18 or older when counted in staffing ratios) and any required education.
The Administrator records the hire date on the file checklist and the training tracker.

The Administrator files the Pennsylvania State Police criminal history application and its date. The application is submitted within 5 working days after hire. For an applicant who has not been a Pennsylvania resident, the FBI check request and date are filed as well. The result and the written hiring-decision evaluation are filed as set out in GR-07.
The Administrator files TB screening documentation and other employee health records according to SH-01. Medical information is kept in a separate confidential section of the file.
The Administrator files orientation records showing each orientation topic, date, hours and signatures (see ST-03).
The Administrator records annual training hours and topics for each employee on the training record (see ST-04).
The Administrator files first aid, Heimlich and CPR certificates and fire safety training records (see ST-05).
The Administrator updates the training tracker within 5 days of any training, clearance or health screening event.
The Administrator reviews the training tracker monthly, schedules training due within the next 60 days, and sends the CEO a list of any overdue items.

Personnel files and training records are stored in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system. Only the CEO, Administrator, human resources designee and authorized regulators may open them.
On request, the Administrator makes personnel and training records available to the Department and to ODP during an inspection or review (see GR-02, REC-02).
When an employee leaves, the Administrator records the separation date, keeps the complete file, and retains it for the period confirmed in REC-02.

Each January the Administrator audits a sample of at least 25 percent of files, or all files if there are fewer than 10 employees, against the file checklist and reports findings to the CEO (see GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Create and keep files, update the tracker, run monthly reviews and the annual file audit, confirm §6400.50 content and retention.
Collect application, qualification and clearance documents and enforce the file checklist.
Review overdue training reports and make sure corrective actions are completed.
Provide accurate documents, copies of certificates and updated information on time.

documentation: Personnel file checklist for each employee
Training record for each employee
Training tracker with due dates
Job descriptions and qualification evidence for CEO, program specialist and direct support staff
Criminal history application and result dates, TB documentation
Annual file audit report

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, relief staff, contractors, volunteers and interns of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set clear standards of conduct and professional boundaries that protect individuals from abuse, exploitation and misuse of their money and property.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires all staff to treat individuals with dignity and to keep professional boundaries. Sexual contact between a staff person and an individual is abuse under 55 Pa. Code §6400.16 and is never permitted, whether or not the individual appears to consent. Staff may not have financial dealings with individuals. They may not give or accept gifts or loans, or use an individual's property. All staff are mandated to report suspected abuse. Violations lead to discipline up to and including termination and a report to the Department.

definitions.definition: The limit that keeps a staff relationship focused on the individual's support and prevents personal, sexual, financial or exploitative relationships.

Borrowing from, lending to, selling to, buying from, or investing with an individual, or using an individual's money, accounts or cards for any purpose other than the individual's own documented purchases.
A person required to report suspected abuse immediately, as set out in GR-03.

procedures: At hire and every year, each employee signs a copy of this policy and the code of conduct. The signed page goes in the personnel file (see ST-06).
Orientation covers professional boundaries, examples of boundary violations, and the duty to report (see ST-03, GR-03).

Staff may not engage in any sexual contact, sexual communication or romantic relationship with an individual. Staff may not photograph or record individuals for personal use or post about them on social media.

Staff may not borrow money from, lend money to, or sell items to individuals. Staff may not accept gifts of money, or gifts of more than nominal value, from individuals or their families. Offered gifts are politely declined and the offer is reported to the Administrator.
Staff may not use an individual's property, money, vehicle, food or accounts for themselves. Staff handle individual funds only as set out in GR-08.

Staff may not take individuals to the staff person's own home, or have individuals babysit, work for or do favors for staff, unless the Administrator has approved in writing as part of the individual's plan.
Staff may not use physical, verbal or psychological abuse, neglect, exploitation or any prohibited procedure (see GR-03, RP-02).

A staff person who sees or suspects a violation reports it immediately to the Administrator or CEO, and follows GR-03 and GR-04 for abuse reporting and incident reporting. If the Administrator or CEO is involved, the staff person reports to the next level of management or directly to the authorities named in GR-03.

The Administrator protects the individual first, by separating the person alleged to have committed the violation from the individual and meeting medical or emotional needs, then follows GR-05 for the investigation.
Staff who report in good faith are protected from retaliation. Retaliation is itself a violation of this policy.

The CEO reviews each substantiated violation and decides on discipline. Discipline ranges from retraining and written warning to termination. Sexual contact with an individual, financial exploitation or abuse results in immediate removal from direct contact and termination.
The CEO reports substantiated violations to the Department as required by GR-04, and documents the report and the discipline in the investigation file.
The Administrator reviews boundary expectations with staff at staff meetings at least twice a year and records attendance.

responsibilities.duty: Follow professional boundaries, never exploit individuals, and report suspected abuse or boundary violations immediately.
Teach this policy, supervise staff conduct, protect individuals and start reporting and investigation steps.
Decide discipline, make sure reports to the Department are made and prevent retaliation.

documentation: Signed code-of-conduct acknowledgment in each personnel file
Orientation and refresher training records on boundaries
Incident reports and investigation files for any violation
Disciplinary action records and reports to the Department

policies.title: Residential Environment, Bedrooms, Bathrooms and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: Administrator, CEO, direct support staff, and maintenance personnel at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To provide a safe, clean, comfortable, accessible and homelike environment that meets Chapter 6400 physical plant limits and never exceeds the licensed capacity.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates each home within the maximum capacity stated on its certificate of compliance (55 Pa. Code §6400.13) and in line with ODP's physical plant guidance. No more than 2 individuals sleep in a bedroom. A single bedroom has at least 80 square feet, and a shared bedroom has at least 60 square feet per person. There is at least 1 toilet for every 4 individuals. A home with only one tub or shower does not exceed a licensed capacity of 4. The agency supplies basic cable, basic internet, a landline telephone that works during a power outage, bedding, towels and toiletries. Accessibility modifications are matched to each person's needs, with landlord consent where the home is leased. The agency complies with ADA Title III (28 CFR Part 36) where applicable.

definitions.definition: The maximum number of individuals stated on the home's certificate of compliance. It may not be exceeded.
A change to the home or its equipment, such as a ramp, grab bar, roll-in shower or door widening, that enables an individual to use the home safely and independently.

procedures: Before the home opens, the CEO and Administrator measure each bedroom and confirm single rooms are at least 80 square feet and shared rooms at least 60 square feet per person. Measurements are recorded on the home's physical plant checklist.
The Administrator assigns no more than 2 individuals to any bedroom. Roommates are matched according to PG-01 and IR-03, with each person's agreement.

The Administrator counts toilets and tubs or showers. The home must have at least 1 toilet for every 4 individuals. If the home has only one tub or shower, the Administrator limits the licensed capacity request and census to no more than 4.
The Administrator checks the census against the certificate of compliance before every admission, and does not admit anyone if that would exceed capacity (see GR-01, PG-01).

Each individual may personalize their bedroom with their own furniture, decorations and belongings, within safety limits. Bedrooms have doors that provide privacy. Any restriction follows IR-02 and RP-01.
The agency provides each individual with clean bedding, towels and toiletries at admission and replaces them as needed, at no charge to the individual.

The agency provides basic cable, basic internet, and a landline telephone that works during a power outage. Individuals have private access to the phone. The Administrator tests the landline monthly, including with the power off, and records the result.

Staff keep the home clean, in good repair, free of hazards, pests and odors, and maintained at a comfortable temperature. The Administrator completes a documented home safety walk-through monthly and fixes hazards promptly.
At admission and when an individual's condition changes, the Administrator and the individual's team review whether the home fits the individual's mobility and sensory needs (see PG-02).

If modifications are needed, the Administrator gets the landlord's written consent where the home is leased, obtains estimates, and arranges for the work. The CEO approves the budget. The Administrator records the request, consent and completion date.
Where ADA Title III applies to the home or its common areas, the CEO reviews barriers and removes them where readily achievable.
The Administrator posts evacuation information and keeps exits clear and usable by every individual (see FS-01, FS-02, H9-01).
The Administrator reports any change to rooms, bathrooms or use of space that could affect capacity or the certificate to the CEO before the change, and the CEO contacts the Department (see GR-01).
Annually, the Administrator completes the physical plant review as part of the self-assessment and reports results to the CEO (see GR-02).

responsibilities.duty: Make sure each home meets plant standards and capacity limits, approve modification budgets and communicate with landlords and the Department.
Measure and assign rooms, check census against capacity, complete monthly walk-throughs, arrange repairs and modifications.
Keep the home clean and safe, report hazards and respect each individual's privacy and personal space.
Make repairs and modifications promptly and keep records of work completed.

documentation: Physical plant checklist with room measurements, toilet and tub counts
Census log compared with the certificate of compliance capacity
Monthly home safety walk-through and landline test records
Accessibility assessments, landlord consents and modification records
Annual physical plant review

policies.title: Transportation and Vehicle Safety
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contractors who drive or accompany individuals in any agency or personal vehicle, and the Administrator who supervises transportation
policies.purpose: To keep individuals safe when they are transported to medical appointments, community activities, work, day services and other places.
policies.policy: No specific Chapter 6400 section has been identified for this topic, so this policy is the agency's own standard of care, and the Administrator confirms any applicable rule in the rule text during the annual policy review. Only drivers who hold a valid driver's license, have insurance and registration for the vehicle, and have completed required background clearances may transport individuals. Drivers know the individual's emergency medical plan, require seat belt use and secure wheelchairs correctly. Vehicle incidents are reported under the agency's incident reporting policy.

definitions.definition: An employee or other person approved by the Administrator in writing to transport individuals after license, insurance and clearance checks.
Use of the manufacturer-approved tie-down and occupant restraint system so a wheelchair and its occupant stay in place during travel.

procedures: Before a person drives individuals, the Administrator verifies and copies a valid driver's license, checks the driving record and confirms the person's criminal history clearances are complete (see GR-07).

The Administrator keeps proof of current registration, inspection and liability insurance for each agency vehicle. For a staff member's personal vehicle used for transport, the Administrator obtains proof of registration and insurance before the first trip and annually after that.
The Administrator checks license status and driving record annually, and removes anyone whose license is suspended or whose record shows unsafe driving from driving duties.

Each authorized driver is trained on the individual's emergency medical plan, communication needs, seizure and choking risks, and behavior support needs before transporting that individual (see IH-02, IH-03, PG-02).
The driver carries or has quick access to a first aid kit, a charged cell phone, the individuals' emergency information and any medications to be given while out (see REC-01, MD-01).
Before each trip, the driver walks around the vehicle, checks tires, lights, mirrors and fuel, and confirms that seat belts and any wheelchair securement equipment work.

Every person in the vehicle wears a seat belt. Individuals with wheelchairs are secured using the correct tie-down points and occupant restraint. Wheelchairs are not used as vehicle seats unless built for transport.
The driver does not use a hand-held phone, does not drive while impaired or fatigued, never leaves individuals unattended in a vehicle, and does not smoke in the vehicle.
Staffing for trips follows each individual's plan and the staffing policy (see ST-02). The driver takes a head count at each departure and arrival.
In a vehicle emergency, the driver pulls over safely, calls 911 if anyone may be hurt, gives first aid, and notifies the Administrator as soon as possible.

The driver and Administrator report any vehicle accident, injury or other event that meets reporting criteria under GR-04 and follow GR-05 as needed. An individual who is missing during transportation is handled under PG-05.
The Administrator has vehicles serviced as the manufacturer recommends, keeps maintenance records, and removes unsafe vehicles from service at once.
The Administrator reviews transportation incidents each quarter as part of incident trend review (see GR-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approve drivers, check licenses, insurance and clearances, keep vehicle records and review incidents.
Drive safely, secure individuals, know emergency plans, perform pre-trip checks and report incidents.
Provide safe vehicles and insurance coverage and review transportation incident trends.

documentation: Driver file with license, driving record, insurance, registration and clearance dates
Vehicle maintenance and inspection records
Pre-trip checklists
Incident reports for vehicle events
Training sign-in for drivers on emergency medical plans and securement

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, relief staff, contractors and volunteers at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among individuals and staff and to protect employees from exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows standard precautions in every home. The agency maintains a written bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030 and offers the Hepatitis B vaccine to staff with exposure risk. The agency teaches handwashing, laundry and sharps handling, excludes ill staff from work as needed, notifies public health authorities when required, and supplies cleaning products and personal protective equipment at no cost to staff.

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all people at all times, treating blood, body fluids, non-intact skin and mucous membranes as potentially infectious.
Gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and similar items worn to prevent contact with infectious material.
Contact of eyes, mouth, mucous membranes, or broken skin, or a needlestick or cut, with blood or other potentially infectious material.

procedures: The CEO and Administrator write, and review at least annually, an exposure control plan that identifies which job duties carry exposure risk and which methods of protection apply.

The agency offers the Hepatitis B vaccine series at no cost to each employee whose duties carry exposure risk, within 10 working days of assignment. An employee who declines signs a declination form, and may change their mind later.

Before working with individuals and every year after that, staff are trained on bloodborne pathogens, standard precautions, PPE use and what to do after an exposure. Training is recorded (see ST-03, ST-04, ST-06).

Staff wash hands with soap and water, or use alcohol-based sanitizer when hands are not visibly soiled, before and after giving care, before preparing food, before and after giving medication, after toileting or diapering, and after removing gloves.
Staff wear gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, wounds or soiled items, and change them between individuals and tasks. Staff wear gowns, masks or eye protection when splashes are likely.

The Administrator keeps a stock of gloves, masks, gowns, disinfectant, hand soap, sanitizer, tissues and cleaning supplies in each home and restocks before it runs out. Staff are never asked to buy their own supplies.

Staff clean and disinfect bathrooms, kitchen surfaces, doorknobs and shared equipment daily and after any contamination, using a product that is labeled to kill the germs of concern and following label directions.

Soiled laundry is handled with gloves, bagged where used, kept away from the body, and washed in hot water with detergent. Each person's clothes and linens are laundered with care to avoid cross-contamination.

Used needles, lancets and other sharps are placed immediately in a puncture-resistant sharps container. Staff never recap, bend or break needles. Full containers are disposed of as required for regulated medical waste (see MD-02).

Staff who have vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or a contagious rash do not work in the home until they are well enough, as directed by the Administrator and their health care provider. The Administrator arranges replacement staff (see SH-01).

When an individual has signs of infection, staff notify the nurse or health care provider, follow the provider's instructions, and take extra precautions such as separate towels, enhanced cleaning, and keeping the person apart from others as advised (see IH-02, IH-03).

After an exposure incident, the employee washes the area right away, tells the Administrator, and receives a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost. The Administrator records the incident and the evaluation.

The Administrator notifies the local or state public health authority of reportable diseases and outbreaks as required, and notifies families and guardians as appropriate. The Administrator reports incidents as required under GR-04.
Medical records related to exposure and vaccination are kept confidential, separate from the personnel file, for the period required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 (see REC-02).
The CEO reviews infection events and exposure incidents quarterly as part of incident review (see GR-06, GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Fund supplies, vaccinations and training, and approve and review the exposure control plan.
Run the exposure control plan, stock supplies, manage staff exclusion, report events and keep records.
Use standard precautions and PPE, handle laundry and sharps safely, and report illness and exposures promptly.
Give guidance on infections, review the exposure control plan and advise on care for ill individuals.

documentation: Written exposure control plan and annual review
Hepatitis B vaccine offer, acceptance or declination forms
Bloodborne pathogen and infection control training records
Exposure incident reports and confidential medical follow-up records
Supply inventory and cleaning logs
Staff illness exclusion records and public health notifications

policies.title: Fire Safety Occupancy Permit, Egress, Smoke Detectors and Inoperative-Alarm Monitoring
policies.applies_to: All community homes operated by [AGENCY NAME] under a certificate of compliance (55 Pa. Code Ch. 6400), all staff, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure each home is lawfully approved for occupancy, that exits are always usable, that smoke detectors and fire alarms work, and that individuals stay protected by a written fire safety monitoring procedure whenever a detector or alarm is inoperative.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] holds a fire safety occupancy permit (certificate of occupancy) from the local building or fire authority for each home before individuals live there (§6400.14). [AGENCY NAME] keeps exits and egress routes unobstructed at all times (§6400.101). [AGENCY NAME] installs, maintains and tests smoke detectors and fire alarms (§6400.110) and keeps fire extinguishers inspected and logged. This policy meets RCG p.82; §6400.110(h) (checklist item 110h): there is a written procedure for fire safety monitoring in the event the smoke detector or fire alarm is inoperative. The procedure is Steps 10 through 17 below. Staff are trained on it during orientation and in annual fire safety training. Test frequency and detector locations follow the rule text, the manufacturer's instructions and the local fire authority's requirements. The Administrator confirms them against the current rule text before each annual self-assessment. Where this policy sets a stricter agency standard, the stricter standard applies.

definitions.definition: The certificate of occupancy issued by the local building or fire authority that approves the home for use as a residence for the number of individuals served.
Any exit, door, hallway, stairway, ramp or path an individual or staff person would use to leave the home in an emergency.
A smoke detector or fire alarm that is not working for any reason, including a dead battery, power loss, a fault or trouble signal, removal, damage, or a system being serviced.
Continuous, documented staff patrol of the home, by awake and alert staff, to detect fire or smoke while automatic detection is out of service.

procedures: Before any individual moves into a new or relocated home, the Administrator obtains the fire safety occupancy permit from the local building or fire authority. The Administrator places a copy in the home's licensing file and the original in the administrative office.

The Administrator records the permit's issue date and any conditions or capacity limits, and ensures licensed capacity never exceeds what the permit and the certificate of compliance allow (see GR-01).

The Administrator reapplies for or renews the permit as the local authority requires and calendars the due dates. The Administrator reports any change to the permit or any local citation to the CEO within 1 business day.

Staff check every exit and egress route at the start of each shift and after any delivery, snow or leaf accumulation, or furniture move. Staff remove any obstruction immediately and note the check on the shift checklist.

No furniture, equipment, storage, vehicle or snow may block an exit door, hallway, stairway, window designated as an emergency exit, or the path to the outside gathering point. Exit doors may not be locked or blocked in a way that keeps an individual from leaving, and any exception is handled only through the rights-restriction process in IR-02 and RP-01.

The Administrator ensures smoke detectors and fire alarms are installed and maintained in the locations the rule text, the local fire authority and the manufacturer require. A written map of detector locations is kept in each home.

Staff test every smoke detector and the fire alarm system at least monthly (agency standard), or more often if the rule text, local authority or manufacturer requires it. Staff replace batteries on the manufacturer's schedule. Staff record the date, the devices tested, the result and their initials on the Smoke Detector/Alarm Test Log.

The Administrator or a designated staff person inspects fire extinguishers monthly for charge, location, accessibility and seals, and logs the result. A qualified vendor services and tags extinguishers at least annually. Any extinguisher that is discharged, damaged or out of date is replaced the same day.

Any staff person who finds a detector or alarm that is not working must tell the Administrator or on-call supervisor immediately, and must not delay for the end of the shift. Staff start the Inoperative-Alarm Monitoring Procedure (Steps 10–17) right away.
Staff on duty confirm whether any other detectors or alarms are affected. Staff record the time of discovery and the device and location involved on the Inoperative Alarm Log.

INOPERATIVE-ALARM MONITORING PROCEDURE (checklist item 110h), Step 10: The staff person who discovers the problem immediately starts a fire watch.
