For the whole time any smoke detector or the fire alarm is inoperative, at least one awake and alert staff person is assigned to patrol every part of the home, including bedrooms, basement, kitchen and attic access, at least every 30 minutes (agency standard). This applies on every shift, including overnight.
Step 11: The patrolling staff person documents every patrol on the Fire Watch Log with the time, areas checked, any concern and initials. The log stays in the home.

Step 12: The staff person checks that the working alarms or detectors elsewhere in the home are functioning and tries to restore the failed device (for example a new battery). If the device cannot be restored, the staff person installs a working temporary battery-operated smoke detector in the affected area, if one is available, and notes this in the log.

Step 13: Within 1 hour of discovery, the staff person notifies the Administrator, who notifies the CEO. If the building's alarm system is monitored or serviced by a vendor, the Administrator calls the vendor the same day to schedule repair. The goal is to repair or replace the device within 24 hours.

Step 14: The Administrator checks that staffing on every shift is enough to carry out the fire watch without leaving individuals unsupervised, and adds staff if needed. The staffing ratios in ST-02 still apply during the fire watch.

Step 15: If the system cannot be restored within 24 hours, the Administrator consults the local fire authority and the agency's ODP licensing representative about additional protective measures and whether any individual needs to be temporarily relocated. Staff continue the fire watch until the system is fully tested and working.

Step 16: After repair, staff test the device and the system, record the date and time service was restored, and the Administrator signs the Inoperative Alarm Log. The Administrator ends the fire watch only after the test is successful.

Step 17: The Administrator reviews each inoperative-alarm event for cause and for repeat problems. The Administrator reports findings in the monthly safety review and the self-assessment (GR-02, GOV-02) and arranges replacement of any device that has failed more than once.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure each home has a current occupancy permit and funds timely repairs and replacement of safety equipment. Is notified of any inoperative alarm.
Obtains and renews the permit, oversees testing and extinguisher inspections, starts and ends the fire watch, schedules repairs, and reviews all logs monthly.
Check exits each shift, test detectors as scheduled, report problems immediately, and carry out and document the fire watch.
Is reachable at all times to take reports of failed alarms and to arrange added staff for fire watch.

documentation: Fire safety occupancy permit and renewals (home licensing file)
Exit and egress check on shift checklist
Smoke Detector/Alarm Test Log and detector location map
Fire extinguisher inspection log and vendor service tags
Inoperative Alarm Log and Fire Watch Log
Vendor repair invoices and notes of contact with the local fire authority

policies.title: Emergency Evacuation Procedures and Emergency Preparedness
policies.applies_to: All community homes, all staff, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure every home has a written, practiced plan for getting every individual to safety in a fire or other emergency, tailored to each person's mobility and needs, with a place to go and a way to get there.
policies.policy: This policy meets RCG p.78; §6400.103 (checklist item 103): [AGENCY NAME] maintains written emergency evacuation procedures for each home that include individual and staff responsibilities, means of transportation and an emergency shelter location. Evacuation routes and steps are tailored to each individual's mobility, communication, sensory and behavioral needs. The procedures also cover loss of power, heat or water, severe weather, and loss of staff. Current emergency contact lists are kept in each home. The procedures are reviewed with staff at orientation, at least annually, and whenever the home, an individual's needs or the staffing changes. Whenever the home serves nine or more individuals, posting requirements in H9-01 also apply.

definitions.definition: The written, home-specific steps staff and individuals follow to leave the home safely, including routes, who assists whom, and where everyone gathers.
A pre-arranged safe place where individuals and staff go when they cannot remain in the home.
A short, person-specific record of how the person is alerted, how far and how fast they can move, what assistance or equipment they need, and any behavioral or sensory concerns.

procedures: The Administrator writes the evacuation procedures for each home before occupancy. They include a floor plan marking every exit, primary and alternate routes, the outside meeting point, and the location of alarms and extinguishers.

The procedures assign responsibilities by role and shift: who calls 911, who assists each individual, who accounts for everyone, who shuts off equipment if safe, and who meets emergency responders. The assignments are written for a daytime shift and an overnight shift with minimum staffing.

Within 7 days of admission and whenever needs change, the program specialist or Administrator completes an individual evacuation profile with the individual's team, including how the person is alerted to an alarm, mobility aids, stair use, and assistance needed. The profile is placed in the individual's record (REC-01).

The procedures state each individual's routes and assistance. For individuals who use wheelchairs or walkers, who have sensory impairments or who need physical help, the procedure shows the exit and method to be used. If an individual cannot evacuate unassisted, the procedure names the staff person or alternate who helps.

The procedures name the emergency shelter location, with the address and a contact name and phone number, and confirm in writing that the location agrees to take individuals. The Administrator verifies the arrangement at least annually.

The procedures state the means of transportation to the shelter, such as the home vehicle, a backup agency vehicle, or a contracted or public transport option, and who drives. Staff plan seating and equipment for individuals with mobility needs (PS-02).

Staff take medications, the emergency information sheet and face sheets, health care supplies, and any needed adaptive equipment when it is safe to do so. A go-bag is kept in each home and checked quarterly.

The Administrator adds a section on loss of power, heat, water or staff. It covers temporary shelter, backup heat or cooling, bottled water, medication and refrigeration needs, how staff call in extra help, and calling the on-call supervisor.

Each home keeps a current emergency contact list by the phone and in the go-bag: 911, the local fire department, the poison control center, the electric, gas and water utilities, the Administrator, the on-call supervisor, the CEO, the nurse, and each individual's guardian or representative.
The Administrator trains each new staff person on the home's evacuation procedures during orientation, before the person works alone (ST-03). Staff sign that they have read the procedures.

Staff practice the procedures through fire drills (FS-03). Drills are used to test whether individual evacuation profiles work. The Administrator updates the procedures whenever a drill shows a problem.

In a real emergency, staff follow the procedures, call 911, move everyone to the meeting point, take a head count against the roster, and stay with individuals. Staff do not let anyone re-enter until the fire department says it is safe.

After any evacuation, the Administrator confirms that all individuals are safe, notifies guardians or representatives, and decides with the CEO whether to move to the emergency shelter. If the event meets an incident category, staff report it under GR-04.

The Administrator reviews the procedures at least annually, after any real evacuation, after a change in an individual's mobility or needs, and after any change to the home or its staffing. Revised versions are dated, and staff are retrained within 14 days.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and updates the procedures, confirms the shelter and transportation arrangements, trains staff, and keeps contact lists current.
Completes and updates each individual's evacuation profile with the team.
Know the procedures and their assigned roles, assist individuals, take head counts, and bring the go-bag.
Approves the emergency shelter arrangement and ensures resources for emergency preparedness.

documentation: Written evacuation procedures with floor plan and routes for each home
Individual evacuation profiles (individual record)
Emergency shelter and transportation agreements, and annual verification notes
Emergency contact list and go-bag checklist
Staff read-and-sign acknowledgement and orientation records
Post-event reviews of any real evacuation

policies.title: Fire Drills
policies.applies_to: All community homes, all staff, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure staff and individuals can evacuate quickly and safely through regular unannounced practice, including at night, and that every problem found is corrected.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] holds an unannounced fire drill in each home at least monthly. A drill is also held during sleeping hours at least every 6 months (§6400.112). Staff record each drill and correct any problems found. Drill times and exits are rotated so staff and individuals practice different situations. Each drill is used to test the evacuation procedures and individual evacuation profiles in FS-02.

definitions.definition: A drill started without advance warning to the staff and individuals in the home. Only the Administrator or designee knows the planned window.
A drill conducted while individuals are normally asleep, to test overnight staffing and how individuals respond when awakened.

procedures: At the start of each year, the Administrator creates a drill schedule for each home. It ensures at least one drill each calendar month, and at least one sleeping-hours drill in each 6-month period. The schedule is kept by the Administrator only and is not shared with direct support staff.

The Administrator varies the day of the week and time of day from month to month, and includes a mix of morning, afternoon, evening, weekend and overnight drills so that every staff person participates over time.
The Administrator or designee rotates the exit used. For each drill, a different exit or route is treated as blocked by fire so staff and individuals practice alternate routes.

The person starting the drill sounds the alarm or uses the smoke detector test button, notes the start time, and observes without directing, so staff and individuals respond as they would in a real fire.

Staff on duty carry out the evacuation procedures in FS-02, assist individuals as in their evacuation profiles, take a head count at the meeting point, and tell the observer when everyone is accounted for.

The observer records the total time to evacuate. The observer also notes which individuals needed prompting or help, whether the alarm was heard, whether exits were clear, and whether staff followed their assigned roles.
For sleeping-hours drills, the observer notes how long individuals took to wake and respond, and whether the awake overnight staff person (ST-02) followed the procedure.

Staff do not use real fire, smoke or heat. If an individual becomes distressed during a drill, staff offer reassurance and support consistent with the person's plan, and report it to the Administrator.

The observer completes the Fire Drill Record the same day. It records the date, time, type (day, evening, overnight), exit used, staff and individuals present, evacuation time, problems found, and the observer's signature.

The Administrator reviews each Fire Drill Record within 3 business days. For any problem, such as a blocked exit, an inaudible alarm, slow evacuation or an individual who did not respond, the Administrator writes the corrective action, the person responsible and the date it was done on the record.

If the problem points to an individual's need, the Administrator tells the program specialist and nurse to update the individual evacuation profile and, if needed, the Person-Centered Plan. If the problem is equipment, the Administrator follows FS-01.
When a drill is missed or late, the Administrator documents the reason, holds the drill as soon as possible, and does not count an announced practice as a drill.
The Administrator reviews drill records monthly against the schedule and reports results in the quality review (GOV-02) and the annual self-assessment (GR-02).
Drill records are kept in each home and available to the ODP licensing representative for review (ST-06, REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Sets the schedule, ensures monthly and 6-month sleeping-hours drills occur, reviews records, and ensures problems are corrected.
Starts the drill, times and observes it, and completes the Fire Drill Record.
Take part in every drill as if it were real, assist individuals, and take the head count.
Update individual evacuation profiles when a drill shows a need.

documentation: Annual drill schedule (Administrator file)
Fire Drill Record for each drill, with problems and corrective actions
Evidence of corrective actions (repair orders, updated profiles, retraining sign-offs)
Monthly review notes

policies.title: Smoking Safety
policies.applies_to: All community homes, all staff, individuals served, and visitors
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of fire and injury from smoking, and to protect individuals' rights while keeping everyone safe.
policies.policy: This policy meets RCG p.88; §6400.114(a) (checklist item 114a): if an individual or staff person smokes at the home, there are written smoking safety procedures. Under §6400.114(b), the procedures must be followed. The procedures are Steps 3 through 12 below. At any home where no individual or staff person smokes, the Administrator documents that fact on the Smoking Status Statement. The Administrator reviews the statement at least annually and whenever an individual moves in or a staff person is hired, and applies this policy as soon as anyone begins to smoke. Smoking safety is part of staff fire safety training (ST-05).

definitions.definition: Cigarettes, cigars, pipes, lighters, matches and similar items, including electronic smoking devices and their chargers.
A specific place, outside the home and away from exits, windows, combustible materials and oxygen storage, where smoking is permitted.

procedures: At admission, and at least annually, the program specialist asks each individual whether they smoke and records the answer in the individual's record. The Administrator asks each new staff person at hire whether they smoke at the home.

The Administrator completes a Smoking Status Statement for each home each year, and any time the answers change. It states whether any individual or staff person smokes at the home. If no one does, it is signed, dated and kept in the home file, and no further smoking procedures are needed until that changes.
If an individual or staff person smokes at the home, the Administrator puts the following written procedures into effect and trains staff on them before smoking continues.

Smoking is permitted only in the designated smoking area outside the home, located away from exits, windows, vents, combustible materials and the vehicles. Smoking is never allowed indoors, in agency vehicles, or in bed.

The designated area has a non-combustible, covered ash receptacle that staff empty daily into a metal container with water, never into trash cans in the home. Staff check the area for smoldering material at the end of each shift.

Smoking materials are stored in a place that is safe for the individual. Where the individual's team has determined that the individual cannot safely manage matches or lighters, staff keep them in a locked place and supervise their use. Any limit on an individual's access is handled as a rights restriction under IR-02 and RP-01, with the team's agreement and documented in the Person-Centered Plan.
Staff do not allow smoking near any oxygen use or storage. Staff post 'No Smoking – Oxygen in Use' signs where oxygen is used.

Staff supervise or assist smoking to the degree needed for each individual, based on the team's assessment of risk, such as seizures, medications that cause drowsiness, mobility problems or poor judgment. The assessment is recorded in the Person-Centered Plan.

Staff who smoke may do so only during breaks, in the designated area and out of sight of individuals if possible, and must never leave individuals unsupervised to smoke or fall below the ratio in ST-02.
Staff enforce no-smoking rules for visitors and explain the designated area.

Staff check smoke detectors in the home monthly (FS-01), and report any smoking-related burns, scorch marks or near misses to the Administrator, who reviews them under the incident procedures in GR-04 through GR-06 and updates the procedures.

The Administrator reviews these procedures annually and offers each individual who smokes information on health effects and, if the person wants it, referral to a cessation program through the health care practitioner.

responsibilities.duty: Completes the Smoking Status Statement, implements smoking procedures if anyone smokes, and monitors compliance.
Assesses each smoker's risk with the team and documents safeguards in the Person-Centered Plan.
Follow the smoking procedures, supervise as the plan requires, empty ash receptacles safely and report concerns.
Advises on medication, oxygen and health risks and offers cessation information.

documentation: Smoking Status Statement for each home (annual)
Written smoking safety procedures (when anyone smokes at the home)
Individual risk assessment in the Person-Centered Plan
Staff training sign-in (ST-05)
Incident reports for smoking-related events

policies.title: Physical Examinations, Health Services and Refusal of Care
policies.applies_to: All individuals served in [AGENCY NAME] community homes, nursing and program staff
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual receives timely physical examinations and routine medical and dental care, and that a refusal of care is respected, followed up and documented.
policies.policy: Each individual has a physical examination within 12 months before admission and annually after that (§6400.141). [AGENCY NAME] supports each individual's access to health services (§6400.144). This policy meets RCG p.92; §6400.143(a) (checklist item 143a): if an individual refuses routine medical or dental examination or treatment, the refusal and continued attempts to train the individual about the need for health care are documented in the individual's record. [AGENCY NAME] has procedures for managing refusals (Steps 8 through 14) that licensing staff may review. A refusal is never treated as permission to stop trying to help. Individuals keep their right to make their own health decisions, and these procedures are applied together with IR-02.

definitions.definition: A medical examination by a licensed physician, physician assistant or certified registered nurse practitioner, documented on a form that records the findings and the individual's health needs.
Preventive and ongoing medical and dental examinations, screenings, immunizations and treatments recommended by the individual's health care practitioner or dentist.
An individual's expressed or demonstrated unwillingness, through words, behavior or avoidance, to take part in an examination or treatment.

procedures: Before admission, the program specialist confirms that the individual has had a physical examination within the previous 12 months. If not, the program specialist arranges one before admission, or as soon as possible with the team's agreement for an emergency placement (EP-01), and documents the date.

The program specialist or nurse records the examination date, practitioner, results, diagnoses, medication orders, dietary needs, limitations and follow-up recommendations in the individual's record (REC-01). The nurse reviews results within 3 business days.
The nurse tracks each individual's next due date and schedules the annual physical at least 30 days before it is due. Staff arrange transportation and support (PS-02).

The program specialist or nurse arranges routine dental care and other practitioner-recommended screenings, vision and hearing checks, and immunizations, and records the dates and outcomes in the record.

Staff accompany an individual to appointments when the individual needs support, bring the current medication list and emergency information, and share any relevant changes with the practitioner (IH-02, IH-03).

After each appointment, staff bring back written orders and instructions. The nurse reviews them, updates medication and treatment records (MD-03) and the Person-Centered Plan, and tells the team and the guardian or representative of significant findings within 1 business day.

Each individual chooses their own health care practitioners and dentists, with support. Staff help the individual understand why care is recommended, in a way that suits how the person communicates (IR-05).

REFUSAL PROCEDURE, Step 8: If an individual refuses an examination, treatment, or appointment, staff stay calm, do not force or coerce the person, and ask what the person's concern is, such as fear, pain, past experience or the setting. Staff never use a restraint or a consequence to get an individual to accept routine care (RP-02).

Step 9: Staff try another approach at once, such as rescheduling, a different practitioner or time, a familiar staff person, a visit to the office beforehand, or use of communication supports, and note what was tried.
Step 10: Staff tell the nurse and program specialist the same day. The nurse notifies the health care practitioner when the refusal affects the person's health, and records any practitioner advice.

Step 11: Staff document the refusal in the individual's record the same day, with the date, the care refused, the reason given, who was present and the attempts made. They also document each continued attempt to train the individual about the need for health care, such as discussions, pictures, visits, peer or family involvement, and the person's response.

Step 12: The program specialist convenes the team within 14 days to review the refusal, plan teaching and support, and decide the next steps. Team decisions are recorded in the Person-Centered Plan (PG-02). The team follows IR-02 for informed consent, and any limit on the person's health decisions can occur only through the rights-restriction process.

Step 13: Staff continue to offer the care at regular intervals and document each attempt. The nurse monitors for health risk and escalates to the practitioner, the guardian or the Administrator if the person's health is at risk.

Step 14: The Administrator reviews all refusals at least quarterly for patterns and for adequate documentation, and reports results to the quality review (GOV-02). Records of refusals are available for licensing staff review.

responsibilities.duty: Tracks due dates, reviews results, communicates with practitioners, and monitors health when care is refused.
Arranges examinations, leads the team review after a refusal, and updates the Person-Centered Plan.
Support appointments, offer teaching without coercion, and document refusals and each attempt the same day.
Ensures appointments are kept and reviews refusal documentation quarterly.

documentation: Physical examination reports and dates (individual record)
Dental and other health care visit records
Refusal documentation, including attempts to train the individual about health care
Team meeting notes and Person-Centered Plan updates
Health care appointment tracking log
Quarterly refusal review notes

policies.title: Emergency Medical Plan and Change of Condition
policies.applies_to: All individuals served in [AGENCY NAME] community homes, nursing and program staff
policies.purpose: To make sure staff know exactly what to do, and who to call, when an individual has a medical emergency or a change in condition, and that the right people are told promptly.
policies.policy: This policy meets RCG p.93; §6400.145 (checklist item 145). [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written emergency medical plan listing (1) the hospital or source of health care that will be used in an emergency, (2) the method of transportation to be used, and an emergency staffing plan. The plan is person-specific, and it reflects each individual's diagnoses, medications, allergies, communication and support needs. The plan supports each individual's access to health services (§6400.144). Staff notify the nurse or health care practitioner and the responsible persons of any change in condition. An inpatient hospital admission is a 24-hour reportable incident and is handled under GR-04 and GR-05.

definitions.definition: The written plan that names the hospital or other source of health care, the transportation method and the emergency staffing arrangements to be used in a medical emergency.
The written arrangement that ensures other individuals in the home stay supervised while a staff person accompanies an individual to the hospital.
A noticeable change in an individual's physical, mental, behavioral or functional status, such as new symptoms, injury, reduced intake, a fall, a seizure change or an unusual change in mood.
The individual's guardian, family member or representative, the supports coordinator, and others the individual has chosen to be notified.

procedures: Within 24 hours of admission, and before any non-emergency admission is complete, the nurse and program specialist write an emergency medical plan for the individual. The plan lists the hospital or source of health care to be used in an emergency, based on the individual's practitioners, insurance, location and preferences.

The plan names the method of transportation. It specifies 911 and ambulance for life-threatening conditions and the agency vehicle or another method for other urgent conditions. It notes any equipment needed for the individual, such as a wheelchair-accessible vehicle (PS-02).

The plan includes an emergency staffing plan that states who accompanies the individual, who stays with the others, how the on-call supervisor is reached, and how additional staff are brought in so ratios are kept (ST-02).

The plan is tailored to the person. It lists diagnoses, allergies, medications, seizure or choking risks (IH-03), communication needs, behavioral supports, guardian and practitioner contacts, and any advance directive. It is attached to the emergency information in the record (REC-01).
A copy of the plan and emergency information is kept where staff can find it at once, and a copy goes with the individual to the hospital or appointment, along with the current medication list.
In a life-threatening emergency, staff call 911 first, give first aid or CPR if trained (ST-05), and then notify the on-call supervisor. Staff do not wait for permission from anyone to call 911.

For a change in condition that is not an emergency, staff tell the nurse or the health care practitioner on the same shift. They describe what was observed, when it began, and what was done, and follow the advice given. If the nurse cannot be reached, staff call the on-call supervisor.

Staff notify the guardian or other responsible persons, and the supports coordinator, promptly after an emergency or significant change in condition, and in any event on the same day. Staff record the time, the person told and what was said.

If an individual is admitted as a hospital inpatient, staff tell the Administrator immediately. It is a 24-hour reportable incident, and the Administrator ensures that the report is entered, as required, within 24 hours (GR-04) and that it is reviewed (GR-05).
Staff accompany or visit the individual at the hospital as needed, share the individual's information, communication needs and preferences, and ask for written discharge instructions.

On return, the nurse reviews discharge instructions within 24 hours, updates medication and treatment records (MD-03), the Person-Centered Plan, and the emergency medical plan, and tells all staff of any new support needs before the next shift.
Staff document every emergency or change of condition in the individual's record the same day, with the date and time, observations, actions taken, who was notified and the outcome.

The nurse reviews each emergency medical plan at least annually, whenever the individual's health or practitioners change, and after any emergency, and updates it. The Administrator checks at least semi-annually that every individual has a current plan.
Staff are trained on the plan for each individual they support during orientation and in annual training (ST-03, ST-04).

responsibilities.duty: Writes and updates the plans with the program specialist, advises staff on changes in condition, and reviews hospital discharge instructions.
Makes sure plans are person-specific, notifies the team and responsible persons, and updates the Person-Centered Plan.
Ensures emergency staffing, reports hospital admissions as incidents within the required time, and verifies that plans are current.
Know each plan, call 911 when needed, report changes in condition, and document actions.

documentation: Person-specific emergency medical plan, including hospital, transportation and emergency staffing plan (individual record)
Emergency information sheet kept at the home and sent with the individual
Notes of change of condition and notifications in the individual record
Incident reports for hospital admissions (GR-04)
Hospital discharge instructions and the nurse's review
Annual plan review dates

policies.title: Nursing Oversight, Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Program Specialist, the designated nurse or health care consultant, and the Administrator at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual's health risks are identified and written into the individual plan. The policy also makes sure that seizure and choking or dysphagia protocols are in place and that staff are trained on them before they work alone. It sets how [AGENCY NAME] oversees health monitoring and coordinates with practitioners and the supports coordinator.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides health services to each individual as required by 55 Pa. Code §6400.144 and the ODP 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide. Each individual's health risks are documented in the individual plan. Where an individual has a seizure disorder, a choking risk or dysphagia, or another significant health risk, the plan contains a written protocol that tells staff what to do. No staff person works alone with an individual until the staff person has been trained on that individual's protocols. [AGENCY NAME] designates a licensed nurse or health care consultant, [NURSE/CONSULTANT NAME], to advise on health monitoring and to review health-related protocols. When an individual has a Medically Complex Condition (MCC), the Administrator confirms the qualification and supervision requirements in ODP Announcement 26-044 and applies them before accepting or continuing to serve that individual. Staff work with the individual's practitioners and the supports coordinator on all health matters. Staff never change a protocol, diet texture, or treatment on their own; changes come only from a practitioner's order or an approved plan revision.

definitions.definition: A diagnosis, condition, behavior or circumstance that could seriously harm the individual's health if it is not monitored or managed, such as seizures, aspiration, diabetes, or pressure injuries.
Difficulty swallowing that raises the risk of choking or aspiration. It is managed through a practitioner-ordered diet texture, positioning and mealtime supervision.
A written, individual-specific plan that describes seizure types, triggers, first-aid steps, rescue medication if ordered, when to call 911, and what to document.
A condition that ODP recognizes as needing additional qualifications or supports. Its requirements are set in ODP Announcement 26-044 and must be confirmed there.
The person-centered plan, including its health-related components, developed with the individual and the supports coordinator.

procedures: Before admission, the Program Specialist reviews the referral packet, physical examination, medication list, and any practitioner orders to identify health risks. This review is documented in the individual's record.

The Program Specialist and the designated nurse or consultant meet within [NUMBER] days of admission and then at least annually. They review each individual's health risks and decide which need a written protocol (seizure, choking/dysphagia, aspiration, diabetes, allergy, or other).

The Program Specialist writes each protocol with the individual, the family or legal representative if applicable, the practitioner, and the supports coordinator. The protocol is filed in the individual plan and a copy is kept in the home's emergency information.

Each seizure protocol states the seizure types and triggers, first-aid steps, timing for calling 911, any practitioner-ordered rescue medication and who may give it, post-seizure observation, and what to document and report.

Each choking or dysphagia protocol states the ordered diet texture and liquid consistency, positioning, pacing, adaptive equipment, level of mealtime supervision, and the emergency response. The protocol is coordinated with the practitioner's or speech-language pathologist's orders and with NU-01.

Before a new or reassigned staff person works alone, the Program Specialist or designated nurse trains the person on each protocol for the individuals they will support. The staff person demonstrates understanding and signs the training record. The training is documented under ST-06.
The Program Specialist posts or places a quick-reference summary of each protocol in a confidential but accessible location in the home, consistent with IR-04.

Staff observe and record health information each shift. This includes seizure activity, meal intake, swallowing difficulty, changes in appearance or behavior, and vital signs if ordered. Staff report concerns to the shift supervisor immediately.
Staff call 911 for any emergency, and then follow IH-02 and GR-04. When a protocol, such as one for a prolonged seizure, requires emergency services, staff do not wait for supervisor approval.
The designated nurse or consultant reviews health monitoring records for each individual with a health-risk protocol at least [quarterly], and advises the Program Specialist about needed changes.

After any seizure that is outside the protocol, any choking event, any aspiration, or any hospital visit, the Program Specialist reviews the protocol within [NUMBER] business days. The Program Specialist then asks the practitioner for any needed order changes and asks the supports coordinator to revise the plan.

The Program Specialist makes sure staff attend practitioner appointments or send complete written information, and that new orders are implemented within the timeframe specified by the practitioner. Staff record orders and follow-up in the individual's record.

For an individual with a Medically Complex Condition, the Administrator confirms the requirements in ODP Announcement 26-044, including qualifications for the nurse or other staff. The Administrator documents this confirmation before services begin and whenever the announcement is updated.
The Program Specialist notifies the supports coordinator within [NUMBER] business days of any significant health change or newly identified risk, so the plan can be updated.
Incidents involving health risks are reported under GR-04 and investigated under GR-05. They are included in the trend review under GR-06.
The Administrator reviews this policy annually and updates protocols when regulations, ODP guidance, or practitioner orders change.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns the designated nurse or consultant, confirms MCC requirements, and makes sure no staff person works alone without protocol training.
Identifies health risks, writes and updates protocols, trains staff, and coordinates with practitioners and the supports coordinator.
Advises on health monitoring, reviews protocols and monitoring records, and trains staff as assigned.
Follow each protocol exactly, observe and document health information, and call 911 and report as required.
Receives health change notifications and updates the individual plan in coordination with the agency.

documentation: Health risk review at admission and annually
Written seizure, choking/dysphagia and other health protocols in the individual plan
Staff training sign-in and competency records for each protocol, kept in personnel files
Shift health observation notes and monitoring logs
Practitioner orders and appointment summaries
Protocol review notes after events
MCC requirement confirmation (ODPANN 26-044), where applicable
Notifications to the supports coordinator

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Specialist, the Administrator, and the certified incident investigator at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To define how [AGENCY NAME] responds to the death of an individual, how it reports and investigates the death, how it notifies the people who must be told, and how the death feeds the agency's mortality review.
policies.policy: The death of an individual is an incident that must be reported within 24 hours of discovery under 55 Pa. Code §6400.18 and the ODP incident management requirements in the ODP 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide. When a death occurs during service, a certified incident investigator investigates it. [AGENCY NAME] notifies the designated persons within 24 hours. The death is reviewed in the agency's mortality review under GOV-02. Staff treat the individual, the family, and housemates with dignity and respect, protect the individual's privacy, and preserve information needed for the investigation.

definitions.definition: The persons who must be told of an incident: the individual's legal representative, family or advocate as applicable and as the individual allows, the supports coordinator, and the Administrative Entity or ODP as required, and any others named in the individual's record.
A person who has completed ODP's certified investigator training and certification and who has no conflict of interest with the incident.
A death that occurs while the individual is receiving [AGENCY NAME] services, including in the home or while with staff in the community.
A structured review of the circumstances, health history, and care preceding a death, to find lessons for the individual's housemates and for the agency.

procedures: A staff person who finds an individual unresponsive calls 911 immediately, starts CPR unless there is a valid do-not-resuscitate order or other documented directive, and follows the emergency medical plan under IH-02.
The staff person notifies the shift supervisor and the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] by phone at [PHONE] right away, and does not wait until the end of the shift.

Staff follow directions of emergency responders and the physician. When the death is declared, staff do not move or clean the area beyond what is needed for safety and dignity, and they preserve medications, records, and equipment.
The Administrator or designee notifies the coroner or medical examiner and law enforcement when responders or the law require it, and gives the information requested.

The Administrator or designee notifies the individual's legal representative or family as soon as possible, in person or by phone, with sensitivity. The notification is made by a staff person who knows the individual, wherever possible.

Within 24 hours of discovery, the Administrator or designee enters the incident report in the ODP incident reporting system (EIM) and notifies the designated persons, including the supports coordinator. The notification is documented with name, date, time, and method.

The Administrator immediately assigns a certified incident investigator who is not involved in the individual's direct care or the death. The investigator begins the investigation under GR-05 and follows the timeframes in ODP's incident management requirements.

Staff who were present write factual statements before the end of their shift or as soon as possible, covering the individual's condition, events, actions taken, and times. They do not alter any record.

The Program Specialist secures the individual's record, medication record, daily notes, and the individual's property, and holds them for the investigation. Property is released to the legal representative or family under GR-08 with a signed inventory.

The Program Specialist and Administrator tell the individual's housemates, in a way each can understand, and arrange emotional support, grief counseling, or a change of routine as needed. Staff update individual plans where a housemate's needs change.
The Administrator offers staff a debrief and support, including referral to an employee assistance resource if available.
The Administrator makes sure the death is entered in the agency's incident log and given to the quality improvement committee for mortality review under GOV-02 and trend review under GR-06.

The Administrator updates the final incident report and files the investigation report and any corrective actions in the incident file. Corrective actions get an owner and due date, and the Administrator confirms completion.
The agency stops room and board charges and handles the funds, final accounting, and discharge records as required by GOV-04, GR-08, PG-04 and REC-02.
The Administrator reviews each death to see whether any rights, abuse, neglect, medication, or restraint issues are involved. If so, the agency also follows GR-03, MD-03 or RP-02.

responsibilities.duty: Respond to the emergency, call 911, report to the supervisor and Administrator immediately, preserve evidence, and write statements.
Reports within 24 hours, makes notifications, assigns the investigator, supports housemates and staff, and makes sure corrective actions are completed.
Conducts an independent investigation and completes the report within required timeframes.
Secures records and property, supports housemates, and updates plans.
Conducts the mortality review and uses findings to improve care.

documentation: Incident report entered within 24 hours of discovery
Notification log showing designated persons notified, date, time, and method
Staff witness statements
Certified investigator's report and corrective action plan
Emergency responder and coroner or medical examiner information
Inventory and release of the individual's property
Mortality review minutes

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers who work at or provide services to individuals at [AGENCY NAME] community homes
policies.purpose: To protect individuals and staff from communicable disease, including tuberculosis (TB), and to protect staff from bloodborne pathogen exposure, by setting health screening, vaccination, exclusion, and recordkeeping practices.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires a health screening, including TB screening, of each person who will work with individuals, as required by the staff health provisions of 55 Pa. Code Chapter 6400, Pennsylvania Department of Health guidance, and ODP direction in effect. The Administrator confirms the current requirements in the regulation text and ODP guidance before the agency begins to hire and at each annual policy review, and keeps the screening forms that meet them. Staff health records are kept in the personnel file and are treated as confidential. Staff who are ill with a communicable disease are excluded from work under PS-03. Where a staff person may be occupationally exposed to blood or other potentially infectious materials, [AGENCY NAME] complies with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, including offering Hepatitis B vaccine at no cost to the employee.

definitions.definition: An evaluation for tuberculosis infection or disease, such as a symptom screen with a skin test, blood test, or other method accepted by the Department of Health or required by ODP.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials during job duties, such as first aid, personal care, or cleaning.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials during work.

procedures: Before the agency hires its first employee and at each annual policy review, the Administrator confirms the current staff health and TB screening requirements in the Chapter 6400 text and applicable Department of Health and ODP guidance, and records the date and source of the check.
Each offer of employment is conditional on completing the required health screening. The Administrator gives the applicant the screening form and instructions at the time of offer.
The applicant has the screening completed by a licensed practitioner or other qualified provider, and returns the signed documentation to the Administrator before working with individuals alone.
The Administrator reviews the documentation for completeness and for any restriction on duties. Questions are directed to the practitioner or the Department of Health.

For TB, the Administrator follows the screening method and frequency required by the confirmed rule text and guidance. If a positive result or symptoms are reported, the staff person is referred to a practitioner and cannot work until cleared in writing.
The Administrator files all screening results and clearance letters in a confidential health section of the personnel file, separate from the general personnel file, under ST-06.

The Administrator tracks due dates for periodic screening on a personnel tracking sheet and reminds staff at least [30] days before the due date. Staff who do not complete screening by the due date are removed from the schedule until it is complete.

Staff must report symptoms of communicable disease, such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or persistent cough, to the supervisor before the shift starts. The supervisor applies the exclusion criteria in PS-03 and arranges coverage under ST-02.
A staff person may return to work when symptom-free for the period set in PS-03 or when cleared by a practitioner, as the exclusion criteria require.
The Administrator identifies job classes with occupational exposure and writes an Exposure Control Plan, reviewed annually, as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires.

The agency offers the Hepatitis B vaccine series at no cost within 10 working days of initial assignment to staff with occupational exposure. Staff who decline sign a declination, and they can change their minds later.
Staff receive bloodborne pathogen training at hire and annually, including how to use gloves, PPE, sharps containers, and cleanup procedures. The training is documented under ST-04 and ST-06.

After any exposure incident, the staff person washes the area at once, reports to the supervisor immediately, and receives a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee. The Administrator documents the incident and maintains the sharps injury log.
The Administrator keeps employee medical records related to exposure confidential and retains them for the period required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 and REC-02.
The Administrator reviews this policy annually and when regulations or ODP and Department of Health guidance change.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms current requirements, makes sure screening is complete before unsupervised work, maintains the Exposure Control Plan, and keeps confidential records.
Check illness reports, apply exclusion criteria, and arrange coverage.
Complete required screening, report symptoms and exposures, and attend training.

documentation: Record of the date and source of the requirement check
Health screening and TB screening documentation in the confidential health section of the personnel file
Screening due-date tracking sheet
Hepatitis B vaccine acceptance or declination forms
Bloodborne pathogen training records
Exposure incident reports and sharps injury log
Exposure Control Plan

policies.title: Medication Administration, Self-Administration and Staff Certification
policies.applies_to: All staff who administer, assist with, or observe medications, the Program Specialist, the designated nurse, and the Administrator at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals receive their medications safely, as prescribed, and only from trained staff. The policy also makes sure each individual's ability to self-administer is assessed and supported.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses each individual's ability to take medications on their own and supports self-administration as required by 55 Pa. Code §6400.161. Only staff who have completed the required medication administration training administer medications to individuals, as required by §6400.169 and §6400.162. Prescription medications are administered as prescribed, as required by §6400.165. The Administrator confirms the course, recertification, and observation requirements in the rule text and ODP guidance, and applies them. Every staff person who handles medications must know the medication error reporting requirements in MD-03. No staff person administers a medication until the training is complete and documented.

definitions.definition: Giving a medication to an individual by the route and dose ordered, and recording it.
An individual's taking their own medication, with or without staff assistance, after an assessment of their ability to do so safely.
The course and observation required by ODP and §6400.169 before and while staff administer medications, including recertification.
Ordered by a licensed practitioner, with the order stating the medication, dose, route, frequency, and time.

procedures: Before the agency assigns any staff person to administer medications, the Administrator confirms the current course, recertification, and observation requirements under §6400.169 and ODP guidance, and records the source and date.

New staff complete the required medication administration course and any required observation or practicum before administering medications alone. The Program Specialist enrolls the staff person and keeps the course certificate.

The Administrator keeps a medication administration roster listing each certified staff person, the course date, the observation date, and the recertification due date. Staff do not administer medications after the due date until recertified.
Staff who are not certified may not administer medications, and the Program Specialist builds the schedule so a certified staff person is on every shift that has medication times.

At admission, and at least annually and after any change in condition, the Program Specialist and the designated nurse or practitioner assess each individual's ability to self-administer. The assessment covers recognizing the medication, knowing the dose and purpose, using the correct route, and understanding the risks.

If the individual can self-administer, the plan states the level of support, such as reminders, set-up, or observation. Staff provide only the support in the plan and document it. If the individual cannot, staff administer the medication.
If an individual's skills change, the Program Specialist re-assesses within [NUMBER] days and updates the plan. The individual's choice to self-administer is respected, in line with IR-02.
Staff administer a medication only if there is a current written order from a practitioner and the label matches the order. Staff compare the order, label, and medication record before every dose.
Staff follow the right-person, right-medication, right-dose, right-route, right-time and right-documentation checks for every dose and wash hands before beginning.

Staff give each dose as prescribed, within the time window the order and agency practice allow, and record it on the medication record at the time of administration. They do not pre-record or record later.

Staff never give a medication prescribed for another person, never change a dose or stop a medication on their own, and never crush or alter a medication unless the practitioner or pharmacist says it is allowed in writing.
If an individual refuses a medication, staff do not force it. They document the refusal, notify the practitioner as directed, and follow MD-03 and IH-01.

When a new medication order, change, or discontinuation is received, the certified staff person verifies it with the practitioner or pharmacy, updates the medication record, and tells the other staff on the shift change.
Staff observe each individual for effects and side effects, and report concerns to the practitioner and the shift supervisor immediately.
The Program Specialist observes each certified staff person's medication administration at least [NUMBER] times per year, documents the observation, and gives corrective training where needed.
Any medication error is handled and reported under MD-03.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms training requirements, maintains the certification roster, and removes uncertified staff from medication duty.
Schedules training and observation, completes self-administration assessments, and updates plans.
Assists with self-administration assessments and answers medication questions.
Administer medications as prescribed, record each dose, and report refusals, side effects, and errors.

documentation: Medication administration training certificates and observation records
Medication certification roster with recertification dates
Self-administration assessments and plan entries
Practitioner orders
Medication record entries for each dose
Refusal and side-effect notes
Annual observation records

policies.title: Medication Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: All staff who store, handle, or dispose of medications, the Program Specialist, and the Administrator at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To keep medications stored securely and to make sure discontinued or expired prescription medications are destroyed safely and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] stores all medications securely as required by 55 Pa. Code §6400.163. Prescription medications that are discontinued or expired are destroyed in a safe manner according to applicable federal and state statutes and regulations. This policy meets 55 Pa. Code §6400.163(h) (RCG p.100, Part B), and describes the procedures for disposing of discontinued or expired medications that licensing staff review. Each disposal is documented. Medications are stored in locked areas, except where an individual's plan allows self-administered medications to be kept in the individual's own space under conditions set in the plan.

definitions.definition: A medication a practitioner has stopped or replaced, or that is no longer needed by the individual.
A medication past the expiration or beyond-use date on its label.
A medication in a federal or state controlled substance schedule, which needs extra counting and disposal safeguards.
A second staff person who observes and signs for the disposal.

procedures: The Administrator designates a locked storage location in each home, such as a locked cabinet or locked box, and controls the keys. Only certified medication staff hold the keys. The Administrator keeps a key log.
Staff store each individual's medication in its original labeled container, separate from other individuals' medications. External-use products are kept apart from internal-use products.
Staff store medications that need refrigeration in a locked container in the refrigerator, separate from food, and check the temperature daily with a thermometer, recording the result.
Staff keep medications away from heat, light, and humidity as directed by the label. Staff never store medications in bathrooms where humidity could damage them, unless the label directs otherwise.

Controlled substances are stored under double lock or an equivalent method, and are counted at each shift change and recorded by two staff when feasible. Any discrepancy is reported at once to the Program Specialist and handled under MD-03.
Where an individual self-administers and keeps medications in their own space, the plan sets how the medication is secured to protect housemates. The Program Specialist checks this monthly.
At least monthly, the Program Specialist inspects each medication storage area. The inspection covers locks, labels, temperatures, expiration dates, and discontinued items, and is documented.

When a practitioner discontinues a medication, or a medication reaches its expiration date, staff remove it from the active supply at once and put it in a locked 'for disposal' container, separate from current medications.

Staff dispose of discontinued or expired prescription medications in a safe manner according to applicable federal and state statutes and regulations. The Administrator chooses the method, such as a pharmacy or drug take-back program, a DEA-authorized collector, or a documented in-home disposal method meeting current federal and state guidance, and keeps a written copy of the method at the home.

Two staff, one of whom is certified for medication administration, perform and witness each disposal. They record the individual's name, medication name and strength, quantity, reason for disposal, method, date, and both signatures on the Medication Disposal Record.

Staff dispose of controlled substances only according to the controlled substance rules in effect, using an authorized collector or take-back method, and with a witness and count recorded on the Disposal Record.
Staff do not dispose of medications in a way that gives other individuals or staff access to them, and never give discontinued medications to other individuals or staff.

When an individual leaves the agency, prescription medications that belong to the individual are sent with the individual or the legal representative with a signed receipt, if allowed by the practitioner's orders and law. Otherwise they are destroyed under this policy, and the disposal is documented.
The Program Specialist reviews the Disposal Record monthly and reconciles it against the medication record, and the Administrator reviews it quarterly.
Missing, spilled, or damaged medications are reported to the Program Specialist immediately and handled under MD-03.

responsibilities.duty: Designates storage, approves the disposal method, controls keys, and reviews disposal records quarterly.
Inspects storage monthly, reconciles disposal records, and corrects problems.
Store medications securely, remove discontinued and expired items, and carry out and document disposal with a witness.

documentation: Medication Disposal Record (individual, medication, strength, quantity, reason, method, date, two signatures)
Written disposal method for each home
Monthly storage inspection records
Refrigerator temperature logs
Controlled substance count records
Key log

policies.title: Medication Records and Medication Errors
policies.applies_to: All staff who administer or oversee medications, the Program Specialist, the Administrator, and the quality improvement committee at every [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, accurate medication record is kept for each individual, and that medication errors are responded to, reported, and reviewed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a medication record for each individual as required by 55 Pa. Code §6400.166. The Administrator confirms the required entries in the rule text and ODP guidance, and the agency's form includes them. Medication errors are responded to and reported as required by §6400.167 and the incident reporting requirements of §6400.18. A medication error involving a practitioner-ordered medication is reported within 72 hours. Staff notify the practitioner and the designated persons. Errors are reviewed in the quarterly incident analysis under GR-06. Staff are not punished for honest, prompt reporting, though repeated or careless errors lead to retraining or other action.

definitions.definition: The individual-specific record of each medication ordered and each dose administered, including entries for refusals and omissions.
A wrong person, medication, dose, route, or time, or an omitted dose, or a dose given without a valid order, or a failure to follow a practitioner's order.
The persons who must be told about an incident, such as the legal representative or family, the supports coordinator, and others named in the individual's record.
A licensed physician, certified registered nurse practitioner, physician assistant, or other licensed prescriber.

procedures: The Program Specialist opens a medication record for each individual at admission, using the agency's Medication Administration Record (MAR). The MAR lists the individual's name, allergies, and each medication with its dose, route, frequency, times, purpose if known, prescriber, and start and stop dates, along with the entries confirmed under §6400.166.

When a medication order changes, the certified staff person updates the MAR from the practitioner's written or verified order and has a second certified staff person or the Program Specialist check the change.

At each administration, the staff person records initials, date, and time directly on the MAR. A signature sheet identifies each set of initials. Refusals, omissions, and reasons are noted on the MAR.

The Program Specialist reviews each MAR at least weekly and the designated nurse or consultant reviews each at least [monthly] for blanks, errors, and consistency with orders. Findings are documented.

The staff person who discovers or makes a medication error stops and makes sure the individual is safe. The staff person calls the practitioner, pharmacist, or poison control as appropriate, and follows the instructions given.
If the individual has symptoms or the instructions require, staff call 911 and follow IH-02.
Staff notify the shift supervisor and the Program Specialist right away, and record the practitioner's instructions and the individual's condition.
Staff notify the practitioner of any medication error as soon as it is discovered, and document the name of the person contacted, the time, and the instructions.
Staff notify the designated persons, including the legal representative or family and the supports coordinator, as soon as possible and within the incident reporting timeframe.

The Administrator or designee reports any error involving a practitioner-ordered medication in the ODP incident reporting system within 72 hours, as required by ODP and §6400.18. Where the error also meets the criteria for a 24-hour incident, such as a hospitalization or death resulting from it, it is reported within 24 hours of discovery under GR-04.

The staff person who made or found the error writes a factual description before the end of the shift, without changing the MAR. The correct entry or an error note is made on the MAR as the agency form directs.

Within [NUMBER] business days, the Program Specialist reviews the error with the staff person to find the cause, such as unclear orders, look-alike packaging, interruptions, or lack of training. The Program Specialist then puts a corrective action in place, which may include retraining, observation, or a process change.
If the error suggests a pattern, a rights violation, neglect, or a supply or storage problem, the Administrator follows GR-05, GR-03, or MD-02 as relevant.

The Administrator compiles all medication errors for the quarterly incident analysis under GR-06, and the quality improvement committee reviews counts, types, causes, and corrective actions under GOV-02.
The agency retains medication records and error documentation with the individual's record under REC-01 and REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Keep the MAR current at each administration, report errors immediately, and carry out instructions from the practitioner.
Reviews MARs weekly, reviews errors with staff, and carries out corrective action.
Reviews MARs and error trends and advises on prevention.
Makes sure reports are filed within 72 hours or 24 hours as applicable, and delivers data to quarterly analysis.
Reviews medication error data and tracks corrective action.

documentation: Medication Administration Record for each individual, with signature sheet
Practitioner orders
Medication error report and incident report in the ODP incident system
Record of notifications to the practitioner and designated persons
Staff statements and corrective action records
Weekly and monthly MAR review notes
Quarterly incident analysis showing medication errors

policies.title: Food, Nutrition, Menus and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All community homes operated by [AGENCY NAME] under 55 Pa. Code Chapter 6400; all direct support staff, the program specialist and the administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual receives nutritious meals and snacks of his or her choosing, that prescribed modified diets and texture requirements are followed exactly, and that regularly scheduled meals are never withheld.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supplies food, food preparation labor and kitchen sanitation in each home. Individuals choose their meals and snacks, and staff support them in shopping, planning and preparing food to the extent each individual wishes and the plan allows. Regularly scheduled meals are never withheld for any reason. Withholding a meal is abuse under §6400.16 and is handled under GR-03. Any diet or texture modification prescribed by a licensed practitioner is written into the individual's plan and followed at every meal and snack. Written menus under §6400.243 are mandatory only in homes serving 9 or more individuals (see H9-02). Homes serving fewer than 9 still document what was offered when an individual's plan, health needs or an ODP/licensing review requires it. This policy is consistent with the ODP Chapter 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide (C59). No official policy checklist items were assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: A diet prescribed by a licensed practitioner that restricts or changes content, such as diabetic, low sodium, allergy-related or calorie controlled.
A prescribed change in food or liquid consistency, such as chopped, ground, pureed or thickened liquids, used to reduce choking or aspiration risk.
Delaying, denying or substituting a regularly scheduled meal as a consequence, punishment, convenience or staffing workaround. This is prohibited and is abuse.
The individual's person-centered plan (Individual Support Plan) and the agency's implementation of it under PG-02.

procedures: At admission and at every plan update, the program specialist records each individual's food preferences, cultural or religious food practices, allergies, and any prescribed modified diet or texture requirement in the individual's record.

The nurse or program specialist obtains any diet or texture order in writing from the prescribing practitioner and files it in the record. The program specialist makes sure the requirement appears in the plan.

Before an individual's first meal, the program specialist or nurse trains all staff assigned to the home on that individual's diet, texture, allergy and choking precautions. The trainer documents the training with signatures and dates.

Each home posts the current diet and texture requirements, allergies and choking precautions in a location out of public view but accessible to staff (for example inside a kitchen cabinet), consistent with IR-04 confidentiality.

Staff ask individuals at least weekly what they want to eat and help them plan menus, shopping and preparation. Group preferences are negotiated under IR-03, and no individual is made to eat a meal he or she did not choose when a reasonable alternative is available.

Staff offer the regularly scheduled meals each day at times that fit individuals' schedules, work and community activities. Meals are available at reasonable times, and individuals who miss a meal due to an activity are offered a meal on return.
Staff never withhold, delay or reduce a regularly scheduled meal for any reason. Any staff member who observes or learns of a withheld meal reports it immediately to the administrator under GR-03.

[AGENCY NAME] supplies the food, the staff labor to prepare it and the supplies needed to keep the kitchen clean. Individuals are not required to buy food from personal funds beyond what they agree to in the room and board agreement (GOV-04).
Staff prepare, serve and store food safely: they wash hands, keep refrigerated items at safe temperatures, date and cover leftovers, discard spoiled food, and keep cleaning chemicals away from food.

Staff clean and sanitize food preparation surfaces, utensils, dishes, the refrigerator and the kitchen floor after each meal. A cleaning schedule is kept in the home, and the program specialist reviews it during monthly home visits.

Staff supervise meals as written in the plan for individuals with choking risk, using the required position, pace, utensils and texture (see IH-03). If an individual coughs, chokes or refuses food, staff follow the emergency medical plan (IH-02) and report as required under GR-04.

If an individual refuses meals, loses or gains weight significantly, or shows signs of swallowing difficulty, staff notify the nurse or program specialist the same day. The nurse arranges practitioner contact under IH-01 and IH-02.

Staff offer snacks and beverages between meals, including at bedtime when the individual wants them, unless a prescribed diet limits them. Any limit must be in the plan and approved under IR-02 and RP-01 if it restricts access to food.
In homes serving 9 or more, staff prepare and follow written daily menus under H9-02 and keep them on file. In smaller homes the program specialist reviews meal records at least monthly.

Staff record in the daily record each individual's meal refusals, modified diet compliance and any incident related to eating. The program specialist reviews these entries monthly and addresses concerns with the individual's team.
The administrator reviews food-related incidents and complaints through GR-06 and GR-09 and corrects any practice that conflicts with this policy.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure each home has adequate food, equipment and staff time, investigates any report of withheld meals under GR-03, and reviews food-related trends.
Records preferences and diet orders, makes sure they are in the plan, trains staff, and checks meal documentation and kitchen sanitation at least monthly.
Obtains and reviews diet and texture orders, advises staff on swallowing and choking precautions, and follows up on weight and intake concerns.
Offer choices, prepare and serve meals as written, follow modified diet and texture requirements, keep the kitchen sanitary, and document and report concerns.

documentation: Written practitioner diet and texture orders in the individual record
Diet, texture and allergy requirements in the plan
Staff training signatures on each individual's dietary requirements
Daily meal and refusal notes
Kitchen cleaning schedule and monthly review notes
Written daily menus (homes serving 9 or more)
Incident reports for food-related events

policies.title: Referral, Admission and Transition In
policies.applies_to: Administrator, program specialist, nursing/health oversight and all direct support staff involved in admissions to any [AGENCY NAME] community home
policies.purpose: To make sure each admission is planned with the individual, the supports coordinator, the individual's team and the county administrative entity, and that health, financial, physical-plant, staffing and capacity requirements are met before the individual moves in.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits an individual only through the referral process coordinated by the individual's supports coordinator, the individual's team and the county administrative entity. Before move-in, [AGENCY NAME] confirms that: (1) the individual had a physical examination within the 12 months before admission (§6400.141, C30); (2) Form DP 1077 (Room and Board) has been completed and signed before admission (ODP Bulletin 00-25-01, C58); (3) the home can meet the staffing in the individual's plan and, at minimum, the ratios of 1 staff per 8 individuals awake and present and 1 per 16 while individuals sleep (§6400.45, C21); and (4) the bedroom arrangement and the licensed capacity on the certificate of compliance fit the individual (C59). The admission respects the individual's choice and the home and community-based settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c). No official policy checklist items were assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: The individual's ODP waiver service coordinator who develops the Individual Support Plan and arranges services.
The county-level entity that operates the waiver program locally on behalf of ODP.
The mandatory ODP room and board form signed before admission, annually, and within 15 days of an emergency placement.
The maximum number of individuals listed on the home's certificate of compliance, which may never be exceeded.

procedures: The administrator receives referrals only from the supports coordinator or the county administrative entity. Referrals from other sources are redirected to the SC and AE.

The administrator or program specialist requests the referral packet: current Individual Support Plan, assessments, behavior support information, medication list, health history, guardian or advocate contact information and any restrictions or risk plans.

The program specialist reviews the packet, meets the individual (and family or guardian when appropriate) and visits with the individual in the home or community before any decision, so that the individual can express a choice.

The administrator confirms in writing that the home has a vacancy within its licensed capacity as shown on the certificate of compliance (GR-01) and that admission will not exceed the maximum capacity.

The administrator and program specialist confirm that the home can meet the staffing and qualifications in the individual's plan, and that the 1:8 awake and 1:16 sleeping minimum ratios will still be met after admission (ST-02). If staffing must be added, it is hired and trained before move-in.

The program specialist reviews bedroom, bathroom and accessibility fit with the individual and current housemates, including bedroom sharing (no more than 2 sleepers per bedroom), bedroom size, toilet and tub/shower counts, and any mobility needs (PS-01). Compatibility is discussed with the team and housemates under IR-03.
The program specialist obtains a physical examination dated within 12 months before admission. If the examination is older, admission is delayed until a new one is completed (IH-01).

The nurse or program specialist obtains medication orders, allergy and diet information, and any health care instructions, and arranges for medications to be in the home and for certified staff to be ready on the first day (MD-01).

Before admission, the administrator or designee completes Form DP 1077 with the individual, family or guardian and the supports coordinator, using the room and board calculation required by ODP (GOV-04). The form is signed and placed in the record before move-in. No move-in occurs without it.

Before move-in, the program specialist gives the individual (and guardian) the written rights information and explains it in an understandable way under IR-01. A residency agreement consistent with the settings requirements is offered and explained.

The program specialist trains all staff assigned to the individual on the plan, behavior support needs, communication methods, health risks, elopement risk and personal preferences before move-in, and documents attendance (PG-02, PG-05).
The program specialist opens the individual's record with the contents required by REC-01 and obtains consents for release of information per REC-02.

On move-in day, staff welcome the individual, review the home's emergency evacuation routes and fire drill procedures with him or her (FS-02, FS-03), and help the individual bring and arrange personal belongings. Staff list belongings and money under GR-08.

The program specialist checks in with the individual daily during the first week and weekly until the team meeting. The program specialist documents adjustment and any concerns, and the team agrees on plan changes.
For an emergency placement the administrator follows EP-01, and Form DP 1077 is completed within 15 days of the placement.
The administrator keeps a copy of the admission checklist (exam date, DP 1077 date, capacity, ratio and bedroom confirmation, rights information, staff training) in the individual's record.

responsibilities.duty: Accepts or declines referrals, confirms capacity, ratio and staffing readiness, and signs the admission checklist.
Conducts pre-admission review, arranges visits, completes records, trains staff and monitors the first weeks of transition.
Confirms the physical examination date, medication orders and health care needs before move-in.
Coordinates referral, team meetings and the Individual Support Plan with [AGENCY NAME].
Complete pre-move-in training, welcome the individual and document early adjustment.

documentation: Referral packet and correspondence with the supports coordinator and AE
Pre-admission visit notes and the individual's stated choice
Physical examination dated within 12 months before admission
Signed Form DP 1077
Capacity, ratio and bedroom fit confirmation
Rights acknowledgment and residency agreement
Staff training sign-in on the individual's plan
Admission checklist

policies.title: Person-Centered Plan, Behavior Support Component and Daily Documentation
policies.applies_to: Program specialist, direct support staff, nursing/health oversight and the administrator for every individual served by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual's plan is implemented as written, that the behavior support component required by the regulation is part of the plan, that service delivery is documented every day, and that the program specialist oversees implementation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] implements each individual's person-centered Individual Support Plan as written. The staffing and staff qualifications in each individual plan are implemented as written, even when they exceed the regulatory minimum ratios (§6400.45(d), C21). Behavior support is a component of the individual plan (§6400.195, C43), and any behavior support is positive, individualized and consistent with RP-01 through RP-03. Staff document daily service delivery for monitoring and billing under GOV-03. The program specialist oversees implementation of every plan.
