This policy follows the person-centered planning requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c) and the ODP Chapter 6400 Regulatory Compliance Guide (C59). No official policy checklist items were assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: The plan developed by the individual's team, led by the supports coordinator, describing the individual's goals, preferences, needs and supports.
The part of the individual plan that describes the individual's behavior-related needs, positive supports and any approved restrictive procedure under the restrictive procedure rules.
Staff entries made each day recording services delivered, activities, health observations, choices offered and incidents.
The qualified staff person (one per 30 individuals) who oversees program planning and plan implementation.

procedures: Within [AGENCY NAME]'s admission process (PG-01), the program specialist obtains the current ISP from the supports coordinator and places it in the individual's record.

The program specialist prepares a plain-language summary of each plan for direct support staff that lists the individual's goals, preferences, staffing level, qualifications of staff required, health and safety needs, communication method and risk plans.
The program specialist trains each assigned staff person on the plan and the summary before working alone with the individual. The training roster is signed and dated and filed under ST-06.

The administrator builds the staffing schedule to match the staffing and qualifications written in each plan, including any support above the 1:8 awake and 1:16 sleeping minimums (ST-02). If a shift cannot be filled as the plan requires, the administrator is notified immediately and arranges coverage. The shortfall is documented and the supports coordinator is informed.

If the individual has a behavior support need, the behavior support component is written into the plan with the team and any behavior professional. It describes positive supports, prevention strategies and responses, and it is consistent with RP-03. Staff are trained on it before they implement it.

Any restrictive procedure or rights restriction proposed in the behavior support component goes through the human rights team and consent process under RP-01, RP-02 and IR-02 before it is used. Prohibited procedures are never used.

Direct support staff record in the daily record, by the end of each shift: the services delivered, the individual's activities and community outings, choices offered, meals and medications noted as required, health observations, behavior events and support used, and any incident.
Daily notes are written in factual, respectful language, are signed and dated, and are made on the day of service. Late entries are labeled as late.
Staff compare daily activities with plan goals and note progress or barriers each week. They bring concerns to the program specialist.

The program specialist visits each home at least monthly (more often when the plan or a change in condition requires) to observe implementation, speak privately with individuals, and review daily notes for completeness.

The program specialist reviews each plan's progress at least quarterly and writes a brief summary. When goals are not met or preferences change, the program specialist asks the supports coordinator to convene the team.

The administrator or program specialist attends the annual plan meeting and any requested team meeting, brings current data, and records any plan changes in the record. Changes are communicated to staff and training is documented before implementation.

Following a significant change in health, behavior or life circumstances, or after an incident, the program specialist reviews whether the plan needs revision and notifies the supports coordinator within a time frame set by the team (GR-05, GR-06).
Daily records are the basis for billing. The billing staff reconcile them with service claims under GOV-03 before submission, and any missing documentation is corrected before billing.
The administrator reviews a sample of daily records and plan implementation at least quarterly as part of quality review (GOV-02) and takes corrective action on any gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Staffs homes as written in each plan, reviews implementation quarterly and acts on gaps.
Oversees plan implementation, trains staff, reviews daily documentation, visits homes monthly and coordinates with the supports coordinator and team.
Contributes health-related plan content and monitors health supports in the plan.
Implement the plan as written, document each day's services, and report problems.

documentation: Current ISP and plan summary in the record
Behavior support component and related consents and human rights team approvals
Staff training roster on the plan
Daily service documentation and notes
Staffing schedules showing plan-required staffing
Program specialist monthly visit notes and quarterly summaries
Team meeting notes and plan changes

policies.title: Community Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff and community homes
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals can access the community, pursue employment, keep relationships and receive visitors without restrictions that are not in the individual's plan, and that staff offer and document these choices.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports each individual's right to participate in community life, to explore and choose employment, to maintain relationships and to have visitors, consistent with the rights listed in §6400.32 (C15) and the home and community-based settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c). No restriction on community access, employment, relationships or visitors is imposed unless it is in the individual's plan and approved under RP-01 and IR-02. Staff are trained in community integration at orientation and annually. Choices and offers are documented. No official policy checklist items were assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: Participation in the same community settings, activities and services used by people who do not have disabilities, chosen by the individual.
The individual's right to be informed about, seek, and choose work, including competitive integrated employment, and to decline or change.
Access to visitors, the community, phone, mail and personal relationships without limits unless a restriction is in the plan and approved through the due process procedure.

procedures: At admission and each plan update, the program specialist asks each individual about interests, community connections, work goals, faith or cultural activities, relationships and preferred activities, and records the answers in the record.
The program specialist makes sure community and employment goals identified by the individual appear in the plan or are raised with the supports coordinator for the team.

Staff offer each individual choices of community activities at least weekly, including outings, volunteering, clubs, worship, shopping and recreation, and support those the individual selects, including transportation under PS-02.

Staff do not require individuals to participate in group outings. Each individual may choose to stay home, go elsewhere or go with a person of his or her choosing, and staffing is arranged to make this possible within the plan.

Staff discuss employment with each individual of working age at least annually and when asked. The program specialist shares information about supported employment, vocational services and local resources, and helps the individual contact the supports coordinator or vocational agency.
[AGENCY NAME] helps individuals who work or volunteer to arrange schedules and transportation, and staff do not discourage employment because of staffing convenience.

Individuals may have visitors at reasonable times of their choosing, with privacy, and may make and receive calls and mail privately. Staff treat visitors respectfully. A limit may be imposed only through the rights restriction process (IR-02, RP-01).
Staff support individuals to maintain relationships with family, friends and chosen partners and to make new connections, and they respect each individual's privacy (IR-04).
If housemates' choices conflict, staff follow IR-03 to negotiate without limiting any individual's rights.

At orientation and annually, the program specialist trains staff on community integration, supporting employment choice, rights to visitors and relationships, and the approach to offering choices (ST-03, ST-04). Attendance is documented.
Staff record in the daily record each offer made, the individual's choice (including declining), the activity done, and barriers (for example transportation or staffing).
The program specialist reviews offers and community participation at least quarterly, looking for individuals with little community time, and raises concerns with the individual and team.
Any individual, family member or guardian who feels access to the community, work or visitors is being restricted may file a complaint under GR-09. The administrator reviews it promptly.
The administrator reviews community integration outcomes during quality review (GOV-02) and addresses barriers.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure staffing, vehicles and schedules allow community and employment choices, and reviews complaints about access.
Gathers preferences, connects individuals to community and employment resources, trains staff and reviews documentation.
Offer choices, support participation, respect visitors and relationships, and document offers and choices.

documentation: Preferences and goals in the record
Daily notes showing offers, choices and activities
Employment discussions and referrals
Staff training roster on community integration
Quarterly review of community participation
Approved rights restrictions, if any

policies.title: Transition, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, program specialist, nursing/health oversight, business office and direct support staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure any transfer, discharge or termination of services is planned with the individual, supports coordinator and team, is preceded by notice and appeal information, protects the individual's records, funds and medications, and applies room and board rules correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discharge or end services for an individual without planning with the individual, the guardian or advocate, the supports coordinator and the team. The individual receives advance written notice and information about how to appeal. Board charges stop on the 8th consecutive day of leave or hospitalization, and room charges stop after more than 30 consecutive days of hospitalization (ODP Bulletin 00-25-01, C58). Records and funds are transferred as the individual or guardian consents (§6400.212, C50, and REC-01/REC-02). Any emergency closure of a home is reported as an incident. This policy follows the settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c). No official policy checklist items were assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: A planned move of an individual to another home, provider or living arrangement, including return to family.
The end of [AGENCY NAME]'s residential services to an individual for any reason.
An unplanned closure or evacuation of a home that forces individuals to relocate (for example fire, flood or loss of utilities).
The room and board rule that stops board charges on the 8th consecutive day of leave or hospitalization and room charges after more than 30 consecutive days of hospitalization.

procedures: When an individual, guardian, supports coordinator or [AGENCY NAME] raises a possible move or discharge, the program specialist notifies the administrator and the supports coordinator the same business day.
The administrator asks the supports coordinator to convene the team to review the reason, the individual's preference, alternatives that would allow the individual to stay, and the new setting.

[AGENCY NAME] does not discharge for convenience, as a punishment, or because the individual exercised rights or filed a complaint. Discharge is considered only when the team agrees, when the individual or guardian requests it, or when health and safety cannot be met in the home and all reasonable alternatives have been tried.

The administrator gives the individual and guardian written notice of the planned discharge, with the reason, the proposed date set as far in advance as practicable and in line with ODP requirements and team agreement, and information on how to appeal, including contact with the county administrative entity and the supports coordinator. The notice is explained in plain language or the individual's communication method.
The administrator copies the notice to the supports coordinator and the county administrative entity and places it in the record.

The program specialist helps the individual visit the new setting where possible, shares the plan, communication needs, preferences and risk plans with the receiving provider, and trains or briefs the receiving staff on request.

The nurse or designee prepares a transition health summary: current medications with last doses, allergies, diet and texture needs, recent health care and follow-up appointments, and any health monitoring. Medications and supplies belonging to the individual go with the individual under MD-02.

The business office stops charging board on the 8th consecutive day of leave or hospitalization and stops room charges after more than 30 consecutive days of hospitalization, and issues a final room and board statement under GOV-04. It refunds any overcharge promptly.

Staff and the program specialist list and return all personal belongings, and the business office closes the individual's funds account, gives the individual or guardian a final accounting, and transfers the balance as directed (GR-08). Both parties sign a receipt.

With the written consent of the individual or guardian, the program specialist transfers a copy of the record needed for continuity of care to the receiving provider (REC-02). [AGENCY NAME] keeps the original record for the required retention period.
The program specialist completes a discharge summary in the record that records the reason, date, destination, notices given, funds and belongings returned, and records released.
If the individual dies, the administrator follows IH-04 instead of this policy.
If the individual leaves without notice, staff follow PG-05.

For an emergency closure of a home, the administrator immediately ensures the safety of individuals under FS-02, relocates them with their supports, notifies guardians and the supports coordinator, and reports the event as an incident within 24 hours under GR-04. Reports are completed in the incident system and reviewed under GR-06.
After discharge, the administrator reviews the transition for lessons learned during quality review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on discharge with the team, issues notices, reports emergency closures and signs off on final accountings.
Plans the transition with the individual, prepares the discharge summary, and coordinates records and belongings.
Prepares the health summary and medication transfer.
Stops room and board charges per rule, closes the funds account and issues the final accounting.
Convene the team, provide appeal information and arrange the new setting.

documentation: Team meeting notes on the proposed discharge
Written discharge notice with appeal information
Transition health summary and medication transfer record
Final room and board statement and funds accounting
Belongings receipt
Signed consent for records transfer
Discharge summary
Incident report for any emergency closure

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff, program specialists and administrators in all community homes
policies.purpose: To make sure staff immediately search for any individual who is missing, notify law enforcement and designated persons when the individual could be in jeopardy, report the incident within 24 hours when required, and plan ahead for individuals at risk of elopement.
policies.policy: When an individual is missing, staff immediately begin a search. A missing-person incident must be reported within 24 hours of discovery (§6400.18, C8) if the individual is missing more than 24 hours, or if the individual could be in jeopardy if missing at all, regardless of how long he or she has been gone. When the individual could be in jeopardy, staff also immediately notify law enforcement and the designated persons. Each individual at risk of elopement has an elopement risk plan in the individual plan. Safety is always weighed against the individual's right to come and go, and any limit must be approved under IR-02 and RP-01. No official policy checklist items were assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: An individual whose whereabouts are unknown when he or she is expected to be present or has not returned as expected, and who cannot be located after a reasonable immediate search.

A situation in which the individual's health or safety could be at risk if missing, for example because of medical need, vulnerability to traffic or weather, inability to communicate or find the way home, or history of danger to self or others.
A section of the individual plan that identifies triggers, warning signs, preventive supports, and the response steps if the individual leaves without staff knowing.
The persons named in the individual's record to be notified, such as the guardian or family, the supports coordinator and the administrator.

procedures: At admission and each plan update, the program specialist assesses elopement risk based on history, behavior, communication, mobility and health, and records it. If there is risk, the team writes an elopement risk plan in the individual plan (PG-02).

The elopement risk plan lists: warning signs, triggers, supervision level, preventive supports, places the person is likely to go, a current photograph and description, and the notification list with phone numbers. The photo and description are kept current and accessible in the home.

The program specialist trains all staff on each individual's elopement risk plan before they work with the individual and documents the training. Staff re-train after any elopement and when the plan changes.
Staff observe the individual's whereabouts at the frequency in the plan. At each shift change, staff verify that every individual is accounted for and record it.

A staff person who finds an individual missing immediately informs the other staff and begins to search the home, grounds, nearby areas and places the person is likely to go. The staff person keeps the required ratio for the remaining individuals under ST-02 by calling in the on-call supervisor if needed.
The staff person calls the administrator or on-call supervisor immediately at [PHONE] to report that a person is missing, so that additional help can be sent.

If the individual could be in jeopardy if missing at all, staff call 911 and law enforcement immediately, without waiting to finish a search. Staff give the individual's name, description, photo, clothing, health and communication needs and last known location.
At the same time, the administrator or on-call supervisor notifies the designated persons: the guardian or family, the supports coordinator and the administrator.

If the individual is not at risk in jeopardy but remains unlocated, staff continue the search and call law enforcement as the elopement risk plan directs, or when the person has been missing for the period set in the plan.
Staff note the time the individual was last seen, the time discovered missing, each search step, each call made and the people contacted, in a written log as events occur.

A staff person reports the incident in the ODP incident system within 24 hours of discovery if the individual was missing more than 24 hours or if the individual could be in jeopardy if missing at all (§6400.18). The administrator reviews the report for accuracy. Incident follow-up is done under GR-04 and GR-05.

When the individual is found, staff greet him or her calmly, check for injuries or illness, call the nurse or practitioner if needed (IH-02), provide food and water, and notify law enforcement and all designated persons that the person has been found.
Staff and the program specialist talk with the individual about what happened, without blame, to understand why the person left. The findings are written in the record.

The program specialist convenes the team within a time set by the team to revise the elopement risk plan, staffing and supports. Any new limit on the individual's freedom to leave goes through RP-01 and IR-02 before use.
The administrator reviews each missing-person event during incident analysis (GR-06) to identify patterns and corrective action, and includes it in quality review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Directs the response, ensures notifications and incident reports, and reviews every event for corrective action.
Assesses risk, writes and updates elopement risk plans with the team, trains staff and debriefs after events.
Provides immediate back-up staffing and support during a search.
Account for individuals at each shift, search immediately, call 911 when jeopardy exists, and document actions.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment and elopement risk plan in the individual plan
Current photo and description
Staff training roster on the risk plan
Shift-change whereabouts log
Search and notification log with times
Incident report submitted within 24 hours
Post-event debrief and plan revision notes

policies.title: Restrictive Procedures Policy, Human Rights Team and Property Restrictions
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] community homes certified under 55 Pa. Code Ch. 6400; all staff, contractors, volunteers, the Human Rights Team, and every individual served
policies.purpose: To state clearly which restrictive procedures [AGENCY NAME] prohibits and which it permits. This policy also states when a permitted procedure may be used, who may authorize it, and how its use is monitored and controlled. It protects each individual's rights, dignity and freedom from unnecessary restriction. It also supports the requirement that any modification of a home and community-based setting right be supported by a specific assessed need.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 55 Pa. Code §6400.192 and Official Checklist Item 192 (RCG p.124): the home shall develop and implement a written policy that (a) defines the prohibition or use of specific types of restrictive procedures, (b) describes the circumstances in which they may be used, (c) names the staff persons who may authorize their use, and (d) sets a mechanism to monitor and control their use. This policy is both agency-wide and individual-specific, as the Regulatory Compliance Guide (RCG) requires.

(a) Prohibition or use. [AGENCY NAME] uses the definition of 'restrictive procedure' in §6400.191. [AGENCY NAME] does not forbid every restrictive procedure. It prohibits every procedure listed in RP-02, which reproduces the prohibited list in the regulation. It permits only two things: (1) emergency physical restraint under RP-02, used solely to protect a person from imminent serious harm; and (2) an individual-specific restrictive procedure, including a restriction on access to or use of personal property, that is written into the individual's plan under PG-02 and RP-03 and approved as described below. Restrictive procedures are never used as punishment, for staff convenience, as a substitute for support, or because of staffing shortages.

(b) Circumstances. An individual-specific restrictive procedure may be used only when all of the following are met: a documented, specific assessed need exists; positive and less intrusive approaches were tried and documented as insufficient (RP-03); the procedure is described in the plan with the specific behavior or condition it addresses; the Human Rights Team has reviewed and approved it; the individual and/or the individual's legal representative has given informed written consent (IR-02); the plan sets data collection to measure effectiveness; the plan sets time limits and a date for review; and the plan states that the procedure will cause no harm to the individual.

(c) Authorization. Only the [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME], acting on the written recommendation of the Program Specialist and after Human Rights Team approval, may authorize an individual-specific restrictive procedure. No other staff person may authorize, add, extend or expand one. In a true emergency only, trained direct support staff may begin an emergency physical restraint. They must immediately notify the supervisor on duty, and RP-02 applies.

(d) Monitoring and control. Every use is logged. The Program Specialist reviews the logs at least monthly. The Human Rights Team reviews all restrictive procedures at its regular meetings. Use is trended under GR-06 and GOV-02. Any use outside this policy is reported as an incident under GR-04 and, where it may constitute abuse, handled under GR-03 and GR-05.

Property restrictions. [AGENCY NAME] does not restrict an individual's access to, or use of, personal property except as §6400.210 allows. A property restriction is treated as an individual-specific restrictive procedure with all the safeguards above. It is limited to the specific item(s) and time needed. It is never imposed on a house-wide basis, and personal property is never withheld, confiscated or removed as a consequence or sanction.

definitions.definition: Has the meaning given in 55 Pa. Code §6400.191. In general, a practice that limits an individual's movement, activity, function, or access to or use of personal property or rights, whether or not the person is protesting it. A restriction that applies to everyone in the home is still a restrictive procedure if it limits an individual's rights.
The committee established by [AGENCY NAME] under §6400.194 that reviews every restrictive procedure before use and on an ongoing basis.
A restrictive procedure written into one individual's plan because of that person's documented assessed need.
A physical hold used without prior planning, only to prevent imminent serious harm, governed by RP-02.
Any limit on an individual's access to, or use of, the individual's own belongings, regulated by §6400.210.

procedures: At adoption and at each annual policy review under GOV-01, the [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms that this policy and RP-02 reflect the current text of §§6400.191, 6400.192, 6400.194 and 6400.210. The confirmation is dated and kept in the policy review file.

[AGENCY NAME] establishes a Human Rights Team in writing. Its members are the Program Specialist, a nurse or health professional, a person with behavior-support training, an individual or family member/advocate, and at least one member who is not an employee or manager of the home. [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] appoints members and records them in the HRT roster. Membership and meeting frequency will be conformed to §6400.194 if the rule requires more than this policy.

The HRT meets at least quarterly. It also meets, in person or by phone, before any new individual-specific restrictive procedure begins. Minutes record attendees, individuals reviewed, decisions, dissent, and follow-up dates.

No individual-specific restrictive procedure may begin without the Program Specialist's written proposal. The proposal includes the assessed need, a description of positive and less intrusive approaches tried, the proposed procedure, data to be collected, time limit, and a review date.

The HRT reviews the proposal. It asks whether the procedure is the least restrictive option, whether positive supports were adequately tried, whether it is safe and respects dignity, and whether it will be reviewed on a set date. The HRT approves, approves with changes, or rejects the proposal in writing.

The Program Specialist explains the proposal to the individual in a way the person understands (IR-05) and to the legal representative and Supports Coordinator, and asks for informed written consent (IR-02). If consent is withheld or withdrawn, the procedure does not begin or stops immediately, and the team reconvenes.

After HRT approval and consent, the [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] signs the authorization. The procedure is entered into the person's plan (PG-02) and the plan's behavior support component (RP-03) before use.
Before applying any restrictive procedure, staff must have been trained on it under RP-03. Staff who have not completed that training may not apply it.

Each time a permitted restrictive procedure is used, the staff person records the date, time, duration, trigger, what was tried first, the person's response, and staff involved. The entry is made on the restrictive procedure log before the end of the shift.

The Program Specialist reviews the logs and the supporting data at least monthly. If the procedure is not reducing the target behavior, is used more often than planned, or is applied outside its limits, the Program Specialist stops it and notifies the [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the HRT within one business day.

The HRT reviews each active restrictive procedure at least quarterly, or sooner if the Program Specialist requests. It decides whether to continue, modify, or discontinue it. A restrictive procedure expires on its review date unless the HRT renews it in writing.

For a restriction on access to or use of personal property, the plan names the specific item(s), the reason, the least intrusive means, the conditions and time for return of access, and the staff person responsible. The procedure is reviewed at least monthly by the Program Specialist. Staff may not take, withhold or hold an individual's property as a sanction. Items held for safety are stored securely, inventoried, and returned as soon as the condition ends.

Any use of a restrictive procedure that is not authorized in the plan, exceeds its limits, or was not approved is reported as an incident under GR-04 within 24 hours of discovery (§6400.18 timeline per RCG). The [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews it for possible abuse under GR-03 and GR-05.
Each individual and legal representative is told of the right to object to a restriction and to use the grievance process (GR-09). Staff help the person file one when asked.

Quarterly, the Program Specialist gives the HRT and the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-02) a summary of the number of restrictive procedures in use, uses, injuries, incidents, and discontinuations.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy; is the only person who authorizes an individual-specific restrictive procedure; appoints the HRT; ensures staff are trained.
Prepares proposals, obtains consent, monitors logs at least monthly, reports to the HRT, and ensures plan revisions.
Reviews, approves, modifies or rejects restrictive procedures; reviews each active procedure at least quarterly.
Use only authorized procedures they are trained in; document every use; report unauthorized use immediately.
Gives or withholds informed consent; may object and file a grievance at any time.

documentation: Written restrictive procedures policy (this policy) with annual review sign-off
HRT roster, meeting minutes and approvals
Restrictive procedure proposals, assessments and signed authorizations
Informed consent forms
Restrictive procedure use logs and monthly Program Specialist review notes
Plan and behavior support component showing the procedure
Property restriction record and inventory
Incident reports for unauthorized use

policies.title: Prohibited Procedures, Physical Restraint and Emergency Restraint
policies.applies_to: All staff, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME] who support individuals in any community home
policies.purpose: To state exactly which procedures are never used with an individual, to allow physical restraint only as a rare, last-resort emergency measure, and to ensure each use is safe, reported, debriefed and reviewed.
policies.policy:
Prohibited procedures (§6400.207). [AGENCY NAME] prohibits, without exception, every procedure listed in 55 Pa. Code §6400.207. These include the following categories: (1) seclusion, meaning placing a person alone in a room or area from which the person is prevented from leaving; (2) aversive conditioning, meaning the use of startling, painful or noxious stimuli to change behavior; (3) pressure point techniques and any technique that inflicts pain to gain compliance; (4) chemical restraint, meaning a drug used to control behavior or restrict movement that is not part of the person's prescribed treatment; (5) mechanical restraint, meaning a device that restricts movement; (6) any restraint that restricts breathing or circulation, including prone (face-down) or supine restraints and any hold that puts pressure on the chest, neck or back; (7) any restraint that is contraindicated by the individual's medical or physical condition; and (8) withholding of meals, sleep, hygiene, medication, communication or contact with family as a consequence. The Administrator will verify this list against the text of §6400.207 at adoption and at every annual review under GOV-01, and any item in the regulation that is not listed here is also prohibited.

Physical restraint (§6400.208). Physical restraint is a restrictive procedure. It is used only as an emergency measure under §6400.209. It is never part of a behavior plan, a routine response, a consequence, or a means of getting a person to comply, and never used for staff convenience or because of staffing shortages. Staff may use only techniques taught in [AGENCY-APPROVED CRISIS INTERVENTION CURRICULUM] and only if they are currently trained and certified in it.

Emergency use (§6400.209). An emergency physical restraint is used only when it is the only way to protect the individual or another person from imminent serious physical harm and less restrictive means (verbal de-escalation, environmental changes, redirection, leaving the person space) have failed or cannot work in time. It is released the moment the imminent danger ends and never continues longer than the limits stated in §6400.209. Staff must treat a restraint used outside these rules as an indicator of abuse. It is reported and investigated under GR-03, GR-04 and GR-05.

Reporting. Every restraint is an incident. The incident is reported under GR-04 within 24 hours of discovery (§6400.18), and in no event later than 72 hours. Every use is debriefed and reviewed under this policy.

definitions.definition: Any hands-on physical hold that restricts an individual's freedom of movement. It does not include physical guidance or contact to help a person with daily activities that the person does not resist.
Medication used to control behavior or restrict movement that is not the standard treatment for the person's condition. It is prohibited.
A device, material or equipment attached to or near the body that restricts movement or normal access to the body. It is prohibited.
Involuntary confinement of a person alone in a room or area from which the person is physically prevented from leaving. It is prohibited.
A real and immediate danger of serious injury to the individual or another person. Property damage alone does not meet this standard.
A structured meeting after a restraint to learn what happened, what could prevent a repeat, and how the person and staff are doing.

procedures: All direct support staff learn the prohibited list during orientation (ST-03) and annually (ST-04) and sign that they understand that no prohibited procedure may be used for any reason. Orientation records are kept under ST-06.

Staff first use positive and de-escalation strategies from the person's behavior support component (RP-03): calm voice, space, redirection, offering choices, removal of triggers, and following the person's communication needs (IR-05).

Only staff with current training in [AGENCY-APPROVED CRISIS INTERVENTION CURRICULUM] may physically restrain a person. If no trained staff are present, staff call 911 and use only non-physical protection, such as clearing the area and moving others to safety.

Staff may begin an emergency restraint only when there is imminent serious harm and no less restrictive way to prevent it. Staff state aloud, calmly, why the hold is used and what the person can do to end it.

During the restraint, one staff person does nothing but watch the person's breathing, color, speech and signs of distress. Staff stop and release immediately if the person has trouble breathing, becomes limp or unresponsive, vomits, or shows pain. No staff person may place weight on the person's chest, back, neck or head.

Staff release the person as soon as the imminent danger ends, and in all cases within the time limit in §6400.209. They never hold a person 'until calm' or to wait out a refusal. If the limit is reached and danger continues, staff call 911.

After release, staff check the person for injury, offer comfort and privacy, and call [NURSE / HEALTH PROFESSIONAL] and 911 for any injury, complaint of pain, or breathing difficulty. Injuries get medical attention under IH-02.
Staff immediately notify the supervisor on duty. The supervisor notifies [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Program Specialist the same day.

The staff person who used or witnessed the restraint completes the Restraint Record before the end of the shift: date, time, location, who was involved, what preceded it, less restrictive efforts used, hold used, start and stop time, monitoring, injuries, the person's response, and notifications.

The staff person enters the incident report under GR-04 within 24 hours of discovery (§6400.18) and in no event later than 72 hours. The Administrator ensures the report is entered and the individual's legal representative and Supports Coordinator are notified per GR-04.

The Administrator reviews every restraint within one business day to decide whether the restraint met §6400.209 and this policy. If it did not, or injury, abuse or neglect is suspected, the matter is treated as suspected abuse under GR-03 and a certified investigation under GR-05 begins. The staff person is removed from direct contact with the individual pending review.

The Program Specialist holds a debrief within two business days with the staff involved and, when the person is willing, with the individual and legal representative. The debrief asks what triggered the event, whether less restrictive steps were missed, what would help prevent it, and what supports the person and staff need. It is documented.

After each restraint, the Program Specialist revises the person's plan and behavior support component as needed (PG-02, RP-03). Two or more restraints of the same individual in 30 days require a team meeting and Human Rights Team review.
The Human Rights Team reviews each emergency restraint at its next meeting (RP-01). The Quality Improvement committee reviews restraint trends monthly or quarterly under GR-06 and GOV-02.

Any use of a prohibited procedure is reported immediately to the Administrator, treated as suspected abuse, and reported under GR-03. Retaliation against any person who reports a restraint concern is prohibited.

responsibilities.duty: Never use prohibited procedures; use de-escalation first; restrain only when trained and only in an emergency; monitor, release promptly, document and report.
Responds to restraint events, ensures safety and medical care, and notifies the Administrator.
Reviews each restraint, leads the debrief, updates the plan and behavior supports.
Ensures training and incident reports, reviews every use, starts abuse reporting and investigation when rules are not followed.
Reviews every restraint and the trend of use.

documentation: Prohibited procedures acknowledgment signed by each staff person
Crisis intervention training certificates
Restraint Record for every use
Incident reports (GR-04) and any investigation (GR-05)
Notification records to legal representative and Supports Coordinator
Debrief notes
Plan and behavior support revisions
HRT minutes
Quarterly restraint trend report

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support and Staff Training
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] direct support staff, the Program Specialist, supervisors, and the planning team for every individual
policies.purpose: To ensure that behavior support is a built-in component of each individual's plan, that positive and least restrictive approaches are always tried first, and that every staff person is trained before and while supporting an individual's behavior.
policies.policy:
Behavior support is a component of each individual's plan (§6400.195). It is developed with the individual, the legal representative if any, the Supports Coordinator and the team, and focuses on understanding the reasons for behavior, teaching new skills, and changing the environment. Positive, person-centered approaches come first. A restrictive procedure may be considered only when positive approaches have been tried and documented as insufficient, and only under RP-01.

All staff are trained in [AGENCY NAME]'s restrictive procedures and behavior support policy (§6400.196), including RP-01, RP-02 and this policy, before working alone with individuals and then annually. Annual training includes the safe and appropriate use of behavior supports. No staff person may carry out a behavior support, or any individual-specific restrictive procedure, until trained on that person's plan. [AGENCY NAME] confirms topics and timing against §6400.196 and applies the stricter requirement. The RCG is the agency's reference for annual training content.

definitions.definition: The section of the individual plan describing a person's behavior supports, as required by §6400.195.
A proactive approach that identifies the reasons for behavior and builds skills, choices and environments that make challenging behavior less needed.
A review of what a behavior communicates and what happens before and after it.
The approach that limits the person's rights and freedom the least while still addressing the need.

procedures: During admission and every plan development or update (PG-01, PG-02), the Program Specialist asks the person and team whether there are behaviors of concern, communication needs, triggers, health or pain causes, trauma history, and what has worked in the past. The Program Specialist records what is learned.

When a behavior of concern is identified, the Program Specialist completes or arranges a functional assessment within [TIMEFRAME, e.g., 30 days] of identification, ruling out medical or pain causes with [NURSE / HEALTH PROFESSIONAL] (IH-03).

The team writes the behavior support component of the plan to include: the behavior described in observable terms; its likely function; the person's preferences and what helps; prevention steps, such as environment, routine and communication changes; skills to be taught; how staff respond at each stage; how data will be collected; how success is measured; and review dates.

The team lists positive strategies first. If a restrictive procedure is proposed, the team documents the positive approaches tried and why they were insufficient, and then follows RP-01. Emergency restraint is never written in as a planned response (RP-02).

The plan is explained to the individual using the person's communication method (IR-05), and the person's agreement or objection is recorded. The individual or legal representative gives informed consent where the plan limits any right (IR-02).

Before working alone with individuals, each new staff person completes training in this policy, RP-01, RP-02 and the prohibited list, as part of orientation (ST-03). The Program Specialist signs off the training date.

Before supporting a person who has a behavior support component, staff are trained on that person's plan: behaviors, triggers, prevention steps, responses, data collection and any authorized restrictive procedure. The Program Specialist or designee delivers it and staff sign the training sheet before working alone with that person.

At least annually, each direct support staff person receives refresher training that includes the safe and appropriate use of behavior supports, de-escalation, the prohibited procedures list, and, if applicable, the crisis intervention curriculum (ST-04). The Administrator confirms the annual training topics and timing against §6400.196.
Staff record behavior data on the data sheet each shift, as written in the plan, and the Program Specialist reviews the data at least monthly. The data is also shared with the HRT and the team.

If data shows no improvement after [TIMEFRAME, e.g., 60 days], an increase in the behavior, or an injury, the Program Specialist reconvenes the team within 10 business days to re-assess and revise the plan, and the HRT is informed.

The Program Specialist reviews each behavior support component at least annually and after every restraint or major incident. Revisions are signed by the team and given to staff, who are retrained on the changes before applying them.
Staff who observe a practice that does not follow this policy report it immediately to the supervisor or Administrator. Practices that may be abuse are reported under GR-03.

The Quality Improvement committee reviews, at least quarterly, the number of individuals with behavior supports, incident trends and training completion (GR-06, GOV-02). The Administrator corrects any gaps within 30 days.

responsibilities.duty: Leads functional assessment and writes the behavior support component; trains staff on each plan; reviews data monthly.
Use positive strategies first, follow the plan exactly, collect data, and complete training.
Checks for medical or pain causes and medication effects.
Ensures training occurs on time, plans are current and corrective actions are taken.
Take part in plan development, consent and review.

documentation: Behavior support component within the individual plan
Functional assessment
Behavior data sheets and monthly review notes
Informed consent forms
Staff training sheets and certificates (orientation, plan-specific, annual)
Team meeting notes on plan revision
Quality Improvement review summaries

policies.title: Individual Records, Content and Emergency Information
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] community homes; all staff who create, use or store individual records
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, accurate, current and confidential record is kept for every individual, and that emergency information is always up to date and immediately available.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for each individual (§6400.212). The record contains the items required by §6400.213, and the [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] checks the record checklist below against the current rule text at adoption and annually. Current emergency information is kept for each individual (§6400.211) and is available to staff and to emergency responders at all times. Records are kept secure, used only as permitted, and protected consistent with privacy safeguards required by 45 CFR 164.530. Entries are legible, dated, signed or initialed with the staff person's name and title, and made at the time of the event or as soon after as practicable. Entries may not be altered or erased. Corrections are made by a single line, with date and initials.

definitions.definition: The set of documents, paper or electronic, kept for one individual under §6400.212 and §6400.213.
Information that staff and responders need in an emergency, kept as required by §6400.211.
The index in the front of each record used to verify all required contents are present.

procedures: The Program Specialist opens a record for each individual on or before the day of admission (PG-01), and attaches the Record Checklist to the front of it.

The Record Checklist, built from §6400.213, covers at least: identifying and demographic information; legal representative and guardianship papers, if any; admission information and referral; the physical examination and health information (IH-01); the individual plan and behavior support component (PG-02, RP-03); medication list and medication administration records (MD-03); consents and releases (REC-02); rights notices signed (IR-01); restrictive procedure approvals and logs (RP-01); incident reports (GR-04); funds and property records (GR-08); the Room and Board Agreement on Form DP 1077 and any related notices (GOV-04); daily documentation; and discharge or transition records (PG-04).

The Program Specialist completes an Emergency Information Sheet for each individual at admission. It lists name and photo; date of birth; address; legal representative and emergency contacts with phone numbers; physician, specialists and preferred hospital; diagnoses; allergies; medications and dosages; health insurance and Medicaid numbers; communication needs; seizure, choking and other risk information; and the Supports Coordinator's name and phone.

The emergency information is kept in a place in each home known to all staff and available at all times, and a copy goes with the individual to the hospital, appointments and community activities where staff accompany the person. If kept electronically, staff have a back-up printed copy.

Staff update the Emergency Information Sheet within one business day of any change in the information it contains (medication, diagnosis, contact, insurance, or risk). The Program Specialist reviews each sheet at least every six months and after each plan update, and records the date and initials.

Direct support staff record services and notes on the daily documentation form each shift, as required in PG-02. The staff person signs and dates every entry, and the supervisor reviews entries at least weekly.

The Program Specialist reviews each individual's record at least quarterly using the Record Checklist, notes what is missing or out of date, and obtains the missing items within 14 days. The Administrator reviews a sample of records each quarter as part of GOV-02.

Paper records are kept in a locked cabinet in a staff-only area of the home or the administrative office. Electronic records require individual log-ins and passwords, and access is limited to people who need the information to do their job. Staff may not remove records from the home except to accompany the individual to a medical or planned appointment, or per REC-02.
Staff may not leave records open or unattended, discuss record content in public areas, or send record information by unsecured email or text. The Administrator provides secure methods.
New staff are trained on record content, documentation standards, confidentiality and emergency information at orientation (ST-03) and annually (ST-04) as privacy training required by 45 CFR 164.530.

If a record is lost, stolen or accessed without authority, the staff person reports it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates, mitigates harm, notifies affected individuals and others as the law requires, and reports an incident where required under GR-04.

When an individual transfers or is discharged, the Program Specialist completes the record, copies only what is authorized for the receiving provider under REC-02, and retains the original under REC-02.

Make accurate, timely, signed entries; keep records secure; report changes in emergency information.
Ensures records comply with §§6400.211-6400.213; reviews samples; manages security and breaches.
Maintains health content of the record and updates medication information.

Emergency Information Sheet with review dates
Daily documentation
Quarterly record review log
Staff training records on documentation and confidentiality
Security incident reports, if any

policies.title: Record Retention, Access and Release of Information
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] administrators, Program Specialists, nurses and all staff who handle or release individual records
policies.purpose: To ensure records are kept for the required time, seen only by those allowed to see them, and released only with proper consent or legal authority, while honoring each individual's right to see their own record.
policies.policy:
Retention. [AGENCY NAME] retains each individual's record for the period set in 55 Pa. Code §6400.215 after the individual's last day of service. The [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirmed the period in the rule text at adoption and enters it on the Record Retention Schedule as [RETENTION PERIOD PER §6400.215]. [AGENCY NAME] does not destroy a record earlier. Where another law or funding rule requires a longer period (for example, Medicaid, HIPAA documentation, or a pending legal matter), the longest period applies. Menu retention of three months applies only to homes serving nine or more individuals (H9-02).

Access. Access to an individual's record is limited under §6400.216 to the individual, the legal representative, staff who need it to serve the person, and authorities and representatives permitted by law, including state licensing and ODP representatives during inspections and monitoring.

Release. Information from a record is released outside those with access only as §6400.217 permits: with a written, signed, dated release from the individual or legal representative, or as the law otherwise requires or permits. Releases meet 45 CFR 164.508. Individuals have the right to inspect and get a copy of their own records under 45 CFR 164.524.

definitions.definition: The period [AGENCY NAME] must keep a record after the individual's last service date, as set in §6400.215 or a longer applicable rule.
A written authorization by the individual or legal representative allowing disclosure of specified information to a specified person or organization.
A person with legal authority to make decisions for an individual, such as a guardian or agent under a power of attorney.
Viewing a record because of the person's role under §6400.216 or the law.

procedures: The [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME] verifies the retention period in §6400.215 at adoption and each annual policy review (GOV-01), enters it on the Record Retention Schedule, and records the date verified.

When an individual leaves the home, the Program Specialist completes the record, marks the final service date, and moves it to the closed-records storage area (locked cabinet or secure electronic archive) within 30 days of discharge.

The Program Specialist labels each closed record with the discharge date and the earliest allowed destruction date (final service date plus the retention period). A record is not destroyed if a complaint, investigation, audit, litigation or an individual's request is pending.

Records due for destruction are listed, approved in writing by the [CEO / ADMINISTRATOR NAME], and destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion. A Destruction Log records the individual's initials or ID, date and method. The log is kept permanently.

The Administrator maintains the Staff Access List for the home: names and roles of staff who may see records. Access is limited to what is necessary for the person's job. Electronic access is turned off the day a staff person leaves.

When an individual or legal representative asks to see or get a copy of the record, staff give the Request for Access form the same day and tell the Administrator. The Administrator arranges a time at the home or provides a copy within 30 days of the request, as 45 CFR 164.524 requires, and may use one 30-day extension only by written notice stating the reason. Staff can help the individual read and understand the record.

If part of a record is withheld, as allowed by 45 CFR 164.524, the Administrator gives written notice of the reason and review rights, and consults [AGENCY COUNSEL / PRIVACY OFFICER] before any denial.

Before releasing information to anyone not authorized by §6400.216, the staff person obtains a Release of Information form signed and dated by the individual or legal representative. The form meets 45 CFR 164.508 and names the information to be disclosed, who discloses and who receives it, the purpose, an expiration date or event, the right to revoke in writing, and a statement that treatment and services do not depend on signing.

The Program Specialist checks the release before sending information. Only the information named is released. The release and the information sent (date, method, staff name) are recorded on the Disclosure Log in the record.

Release to the Supports Coordinator, ODP, the Department's licensing staff and other authorities needed for services, payment, health care operations or required by law follows IR-04. Staff do not delay a release needed for emergency medical care. They document the disclosure afterward.

A staff person who receives a subpoena, court order or request from police, a reporter or a family member without authority does not release anything. The staff person refers it to the Administrator, who consults [AGENCY COUNSEL / PRIVACY OFFICER] and responds in line with law.
When an individual is transferred, the Program Specialist sends the receiving provider only the records authorized by a signed release or permitted by law, with a transfer record in the file (PG-04).
At orientation (ST-03) and annually (ST-04), all staff are trained on access, release and confidentiality. The Administrator reviews the Disclosure Log and Staff Access List at least quarterly.

Any improper access or disclosure is reported immediately to the Administrator, investigated, documented, corrected, and handled as a privacy breach and, if required, as an incident under GR-04 and IR-04.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies the retention period; approves destruction; manages access list; answers access requests; handles breaches.
Closes and archives records; obtains valid releases; maintains the Disclosure Log.
Access only needed information; never release records without authority; refer requests to the supervisor.
Advises on subpoenas, denials of access and privacy questions.
